That this House deplores the continuing failure of the Liberal government to do anything whatsoever about the unemployment and misery caused by its inane mismanagement of the economy.

subsubtopic: CHALLENGE TO GOVERNMENT-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:

That this House condemns the Liberal government for its lack of an economic program which would stimulate our failing economy and provide incentive to business to create employment opportunity, and, further, challenges the government to present its policies before the Canadian electorate to determine whether Canadians desire that kind of haphazard approach to economic problems.

That the Minister of Defence immediately look into this shameful situation in which thousands of members of our armed forces are receiving eye care from inadequately trained ophthalmic technicians, and immediately rectify this idiotic practice and assign doctors of optometry to care for the visual needs of our servicemen.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND MEDICAL CARE
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. On Friday my colleague from Hillsborough put a question to the Minister of Finance with regard to the recent story in the Toronto Star to the effect that the spending cuts by the federal government in post-secondary education and medical care were now going to amount to a net $4.5 billion. On Friday the minister said that he could not confirm those figures. Has his department now let him in on the secret, and can he confirm that figure today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the first point to make is that I am not proposing any reductions in our support for post-secondary education or medical health care.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
That has not been our proposition in the past, or at the present time.
What I have put before the provinces is the intention of the federal government to eliminate the revenue guarantee which even the premiers in their communique last summer did not include as part of the federal support for medical care and post-secondary education.
I would draw the attention of my hon. friend to the budget paper entitled "Fiscal Arrangements in the Eighties", in which it is stated that the expenditure plan presented in last year's budget provided for savings and transfers to provinces and territories of about $500 million in 1982-83 and $1 billion in 1983-84 and subsequent years. There is no question that we are attempting to achieve savings in the transfers through the elimination of the revenue guarantee.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS FUNDING FOR POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION AND MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister has failed, for the second time, to answer the question. The question was if the figure mentioned in the Toronto Star article on Friday, of $4.5 billion net cut, was an accurate figure, and would he be

February 1, 1982
Oral Questions
prepared to confirm that figure today. For the purpose of my supplementary question I will assume that it was of that order.

In the original estimate in the budget the minister referred to a net cut of $1.9 billion. Presumably that was the maximum amount of net cut that he felt the provinces could stand without cutting services in post-secondary education and medical health. That figure has now been increased, first by a mistake on the minister's part to $2.6 billion, then to $4.5 billion as a result of the announcement on Friday.
Since the provinces cannot count on the figures which the minister or his department put out to the public, would he be prepared to enter into a new form of revenue guarantee which would limit the net cutbacks by the federal government in these two very important areas of spending to $1.9 billion, because the provinces cannot count on the figures that the minister has been throwing around in the past two weeks?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we have had several meetings with the provinces and the provincial ministers of finance. They have not been left in any doubt about the extent of the savings that the Government of Canada intends to achieve. These were discussed very intensively in the meeting which I had with the ministers of finance in Ottawa not very long ago. They have all the up-to-date figures.
Why do you not give us the up-to-date figures?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: As I have stated to the hon. member, look at the budget paper entitled "Fiscal Arrangements in the Eighties" and he will find that I talk about a $500 million saving in 1982-83 and a $1 billion saving in 1983-84 and subsequent years. I announced subsequently that it was the intention of the government to eliminate the revenue guarantee. That is the total saving that is being sought in the EPF transfers. I would tell the hon. member that, despite the cut of the revenue guarantee, the total system of transfers will increase on an annual basis to the provinces by about 12 per cent per year. I believe that is a creditable rate of increase in view of the restraint that is being imposed upon the Government of Canada.

Madam Speaker, twice the minister has referred to the budget papers, but because of mistakes 11 days after the budget, and because of new figures which came out last week, those budget papers are completely out of date.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT NATIONAL CONFERENCES BE HELD ON MEDICAL CARE AND POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
REQUEST THAT NATIONAL CONFERENCES BE HELD ON MEDICAL CARE AND POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, let me approach this from another angle, it seems that the cart is being put before the horse. The minister is proposing to cut spending in two very important areas. He is prepared to risk major cutbacks in medical care and post-secondary education. Rather than rush into this on a unilateral basis and force spending cuts and service cuts on the provinces, would the minister and the government consider entering into two or three national conferences on health and post-secondary education so that we can set out the national objectives of the various levels of government in these two important areas before we cut spending, and before we cause closures of hospitals and cutbacks in post-secondary education?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST THAT NATIONAL CONFERENCES BE HELD ON MEDICAL CARE AND POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me repeat once again the statement that there are no cuts proposed in the federal support for medicare or post-secondary education. For example, shortly after the budget papers were released, the president of the Canadian Medical Association stated at the association's annual meeting in Halifax that it would be wrong to claim that the budget would bring about any reduction in support for medical care. He said that would be wrong, and it is wrong. The same is true about post-secondary education.
The hon. member has asked for conferences. It has been laid out that it is the intention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to conduct consultations with provinces on program conditions, and it is also laid out that the Secretary of State will conduct discussions with the provinces in order to see how national objectives could best be met in that field.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT NATIONAL CONFERENCES BE HELD ON MEDICAL CARE AND POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext: Why not do that first?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST THAT NATIONAL CONFERENCES BE HELD ON MEDICAL CARE AND POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext: The hon. member suggests that these discussions ought to take place first. There is no logic to that because the proposed savings to the provinces will not affect in any way whatsoever our support either for medical care or post-secondary education, and that is widely understood by the client groups in the country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance, who says there will be no cuts, just that there will be $4.5 billion less for the provinces to use for health and education services.
Let me refer to a statement the minister made in this House. It has to do with the reliability of this minister of hocus-pocus, the minister of Rubik's cube, and the reliability of his figures.

Stick to your lines, Joe.
February 1, 1982

On January 26 the minister stated in this Elouse:
Twelve million Canadians will have less taxes to pay, about 3.5 million will pay the same amount and about 800,000 will pay more taxes. These are the
facts.
By those figures the minister is claiming that 16.1 million Canadians will pay 1982 personal income taxes. The figures of the Department of National Revenue for the last year for which figures are available, 1980, indicate that in that year fewer than ten million Canadians paid federal tax.
My question to the minister flows from the fact that the minister is now claiming that some six million Canadians who did not pay federal tax in 1980 will be paying federal tax as a result of his budget. Will he tell us how he arranged that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, all the information with respect to the tax cuts are contained in the budget papers.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am very pleased that the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has raised again the question of tax relief and tax benefits. Last Friday he alleged that it was unjustified for the government-
Watch out, Pinnochio!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: -to claim any credit for the retention of indexation. I had stated in the budget speech, and subsequently, that the equivalent of $3 billion worth of tax relief had been distributed to Canadians through the retention of indexation.
Malarkey!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. Leader of the Opposition contested that rather violently. I should like to refer him to the ad on indexation which his party put out before the October budget. This is addressed to the taxpayers of Canada.
Order. Order.
You are scraping the bottom of the barrel. Why don't you read the whole thing?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: It says that in 1980 if your income was $15,000 per year you would have to pay $217 more income tax with de-indexing. It goes on to talk about $25,000, $35,000, $50,000-
Order!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
-showing the amounts that taxpayers would have to pay in addition, in the absence of indexation. The hon. member goes on, or the ad goes on to say that that is how much more you would pay. I am telling him that the budget that was produced on November 12 saved the taxpayer these amounts, which the hon. member said would be lost.
Oral Questions
Madam Speaker, I guess the minister is saying, "If you ask me a question this week I will give you an answer nobody can believe next week."
Hear, hear!
To six million Canadians he is saying, "You didn't pay any tax before and, as a result of my budget, you will pay tax, and that is a cut, folks." That is what the Minister of Finance says.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, let me ask the innocent lamb who is the Minister of National Revenue whether he agrees with his colleague, the Minister of Finance, that as a result of this budget, six million Canadians who were not paying taxes in 1980 will be paying taxes in 1982?

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has referred to Rubik's cube. He would know, because of course he is just a plain old square!
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!
Bring the hook.

The Minister of Finance has laid out clearly the savings to Canadians as a result of this budget-not simply the indexation but the change in the tax structure, the increase in the child tax credit, the reduction in unemployment insurance premiums, and all these things which add up to savings for Canadians. I would say to Canadians that, instead of listening to the hocus-pocus that is tried on that side of the House, they should look at their pay cheques at the end of the month and they will see the reductions.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, better a plain old square than a government whose figures and whose word cannot be believed by any Canadian in this land.
Hear, hear!

If the minister is unwilling to explain those six million new Canadian taxpayers as a result of his government's budget, perhaps I can try him out province by province. Let us start with Newfoundland. The minister has said that there will be a reduction in taxes for 250,000 people in Newfoundland. That is what he said. In 1980 in Newfoundland fewer than
200,000	paid federal tax. Will the Minister of National Revenue explain what his colleague has done to impose on 50,000

February 1, 1982
Oral Questions
Newfoundlanders who were not paying tax in 1980, tax this year, as a result of the Liberal government's budget? Could he explain that to us?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: By your own figures.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, a representative of a knowledgeable chartered accountant's firm in St. John's says this budget is better for Newfoundland than any other part of the country. The fact is that by far the majority of people will see their incomes improved as a result of the budget. I say to the right hon. gentleman again that all people have to do-
-is look at their pay cheques!
-is look at their pay cheques at the end of the month, and not worry about figures.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FIRST MINISTER'S CONFERENCE-POLICY FOLLOWED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. It concerns the First Ministers' Conference which opens tomorrow. It is very clear that a majority of provincial premiers are deeply concerned about unemployment and the general increase in job insecurity throughout the country. Considering that the minister has said throughout last week that he has no intention of changing his basic monetary and fiscal approach on the one hand, but on the other hand that he plans to listen and be open-minded to what the premiers have to say, does the Government of Canada plan to listen seriously to what the premiers have to say about unemployment programs? Specifically, is the government prepared to change its mind about its monetary and fiscal approach which has produced more than one million unemployed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FIRST MINISTER'S CONFERENCE-POLICY FOLLOWED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I said on Friday that I would be interested to hear whether the premiers had an alternative to the current economic policy followed by the government. The policy now being followed is based upon the necessity of reducing inflationary pressures in the economy which are the main obstacles to improved job creation and improved growth in the country. Unless we have a better control of the inflation rate, I believe that we will have no possibility of getting the jobs we require in the future. I believe it is worth taking the necessary relatively short-term measures which are required in order to build a strong economy for the future; that is my approach. If the premiers can bring forward
a better alternative which is convincing, of course the government is quite prepared to examine it with great interest and attention.

subsubtopic: FIRST MINISTER'S CONFERENCE-POLICY FOLLOWED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: But presumably unwilling to change its monetary and fiscal approach. That was the question I asked.

Madam Speaker, considering the approach currently pursued by the Government of Canada, the approach which has produced ten million unemployed in the United States under Ronald Reagan and has now produced three million unemployed, and rising, in Great Britain under Margaret Thatcher, is the Minister of Finance saying to the people of Canada that he is prepared to continue with this high interest rate policy even if it leads to this abysmal direction for the people of Canada? Does the minister really have in mind constant levels of unemployment? If so, will he say it openly to the people of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, that is not what I have in mind. I have in mind lower unemployment rates. The objective is to get unemployment down. The hon. member must know the experience has been that countries with lower rates of inflation have lower rates of unemployment. It no accident that countries such as Japan, Switzerland, and Wes( Germany, with relatively low rates of inflation, have the lowest rates of unemployment. That is a clear link. Until we break the inflation spiral, the prospect of obtaining jobs as quickly as we would like does not seem to be very close. This is what I have in mind.

Madam Speaker, countries like Japan and Switzerland particularly and persistently have pursued lower interest rate policies. As the minister well knows, the government of France today has an officially established low interest rate policy because it is concerned about both inflation and unemployment. The Canadian government has not produced results on either side of the economic ledger, either in terms of inflation or unemployment. The government has been an unmitigated disaster, and every Canadian knows it.
Hear, hear!

I see the minister smiling; it reflects his deep concern. In an interview published in Le Devoir this morning the minister said, "Everyone has to accept some change in his life." What does the minister explicitly mean by this? Does he mean collecting an unemployment insurance cheque instead of a pay cheque? Does he mean foreclosure on a home instead of the security of a home? Does he mean no job at the end of the academic year instead of a job with a BA.? If this is what the minister means by change, why is he
February 1, 1982

not at least honest like Margaret Thatcher and have the courage to put things out in the open, instead of using weasel words like "some change" in their lives?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member talks about a high interest rate policy as if it were something separate from the high inflation we are experiencing. They are both one and the same. It is evident that it will be impossible to make substantial progress in reducing interest rates anywhere, unless the rate of inflation comes down. The hon. member knows perfectly well. For example, he quoted in the House at least once or twice the new socialist government in France. He knows what has happened there. It attempted to stimulate the economy. Its prices went up. It brought in controls but, lo and behold, while all this was happening unemployment was rising as well, not going down. He has it a bit mixed up.
Not as a result of those programs, and the minister knows it.

subsubtopic: COMPLIANCE WITH CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES BY MINISTER OF STATE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. On September 22 the Prime Minister appointed Senator Jack Austin to the ministry. The Assistant Deputy Registrar General confirmed this morning that Senator Austin has not yet complied with the conflict of interest guidelines by filing the required declarations with the Conflict of Interest Public Registry. In view of the fact that Senator Austin has responsibility for the Canadian Development Corporation, a Crown corporation investing in private commercial concerns across the country, it is particularly important that compliance be made forthwith. Today, without a doubt, the farming industry in Canada is facing its worst financial crisis since the great depression. Last year alone, some 260 farmers were forced into bankruptcy because of the high interest rate policy while others were pushed into forced sales which, in some cases, ended farming establishments which had been in families for generations.
When we look at recent government responses to this rapidly worsening situation, we are left with the fact that, when the government acted, it offered too little, too late. A good example of just such an offer is the bill we now have before us, Bill C-88, respecting loans to farmers. Another example, of course,
Farm Loans
is the budget itself. However, despite the drawbacks of this bill, which I will go into shortly, we support Bill C-88 in principle because it offers more financial aid to our farmers, and that is good. The bill, however, does not go far enough and we have some useful suggestions that we believe will strengthen this legislation and make it more helpful to the farming community.
Generally speaking, we think the Farm Credit Corporation has provided a valuable service to the agriculture industry over the years. Its financial assistance has been invaluable and we support the corporation in its efforts to extend financial assistance to the industry. By giving the Farm Credit Corporation authority to borrow funds from the private marketplace, some desperately needed money will be made available to farmers. With the FCC almost drained of funds to lend, any new injection of money, however small, is obviously a very good thing.
However, beyond this favourable principle of increasing resources, there are problems with this bill. We are very concerned about the amount of funds being made available by the government to farmers through the Farm Credit Corporation. Simply put, we believe, as the industry does, that the corporation is massively underbudgeted. We wonder why only $50 million was offered by the government in its November 12 budget when it knows a more realistic federal contribution is at least ten times that much, $500 million. Some, like the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, would say $1 billion is needed. In fact, every agricultural group has called for a higher and more reasonable level of federal funding. Hopefully, the government will finally recognize this obvious need and increase its aid to a more realistic level.
Of course, allowing the FCC to borrow from private sources will increase its resources, but we hope this move does not mean the government is planning to back out of its financial responsibilities. We need strong assurances that the FCC borrowing authority is supplementary borrowing only and is in no way going to replace direct federal funding. Perhaps when this legislation enters committee the minister will give us these necessary assurances.
Let me say that increased direct federal funding is necessary because allowing the FCC to borrow on the open market does not solve the immediate problems of underfunding. Bill C-88, simply put, does not address the very real problem of shortterm relief. We all know that relief is needed, in many cases right now, in the short term.
The government has helped to solve the long-range funding problems, but it has not even mentioned short-term relief problems. This is why the $50 million offered by the government is so inadequate, considering the average farm loan today is for $100,000. This money will be gone in no time, leaving those in immediate difficulties in much the same situation they find themselves in now, facing imminent bankruptcy. This is an important element completely absent from the legislation,

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
so again, during committee stage, perhaps we can get some positive answers to the problem.
We also question why this type of legislation was not introduced earlier. It is long overdue and, for that reason, it is welcome; but again, it does not adequately help farmers overcome their massive financial difficulties. It is too little and too late.
We would also ask, as my colleagues from Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) and Elgin (Mr. Wise) asked earlier, why no mention was made of offering further aid to farmers by way of placing a moratorium on farm bankruptcies. While this is not a solution to the problem, it could go a long way in helping to save farmers from very tough times.
The government has said time and time again that there is a need for economic restraint and that spending cuts have meant reducing available funds for many programs, including aid for our farmers. However, for an area of the economy as important as the agriculture industry is to the economy as a whole, the government's policies are simply ignoring the needs of farmers to create a thriving industry.
The government is only paying lip service to agricultural problems while its tightfisted monetary policy is bringing our farming industry to its knees by creating and maintaining high interest rates and record-high inflation, the very elements that are killing the industry. The government has long ago lost the power or strength of argument to justify its economic restraint policies. We only have to look at the agricultural industry to see how wrong and misguided those policies are to the wellbeing of all Canadians.
Looking to other elements of the legislation before us, we have to ask why the government sees the need to expand the board of the FCC to seven members. We can only hope that these new members are chosen because of their expertise in farming and financial matters, and not because of their past voting habits. Increasing the number may only create greater administrative costs while not necessarily benefiting the agricultural industry itself.
Let's not fool ourselves here. Farm credit loans are not handouts or charity. Each loan is paid back in full, with interest. Loans are a very major part of operating a farm, and dependence on long-term loans has become even greater in recent years. While prices have remained relatively steady over the years, operating costs, such as machinery, livestock feed, pesticides, fertilizer and, of course, interest rates on loans, have all skyrocketed. Therefore, many farmers find themselves coming up short in their current cash flow, even though they have large amounts of capital tied up in machinery and property. A much greater financial effort is therefore needed to help our farmers remain in business.
There are also serious questions concerning how the Farm Credit Corporation is administering the resources at its disposal and how it is treating applicants. Several farmers in my constituency have complained about what they feel is the arrogant, unsympathetic and downright rude attitude they have received in their dealings with some-and I stress some-
FCC field workers. Many farmers I have talked to are very angry and upset to be treated this way when they apply for assistance, which often means the difference between bankruptcy and keeping a slim hold on their livelihood.
I believe very strongly that the FCC should take a hard look at how its program is being administered in order to make sure it is running properly. It is very important to treat our farming community with the respect and dignity deserving of such a hard-working and fundamental sector of our economy.
As I said at the outset, we support this legislation before us. We believe Bill C-88 is a worth-while measure for long-range funding of the FCC and, as my colleagues and I have stressed throughout the debate, as long as the federal government does not lower its direct contributions, we back the bill in principle.
We also hope that the government will guarantee the bonds floated by the FCC so they can be sold more quickly and benefit our farmers that much sooner.
If we want to have a strong agricultural industry, able to produce food efficiently and provide for a reasonable return, the government must be prepared to do its part by creating the necessary atmosphere of growth and recovery. Bill C-88 is a start and if the government looks closely at what we are calling for, we will go a long way in reviving this economically depressed industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise this afternoon to speak briefly on Bill C-88 respecting farm loans. The purpose of the bill is to ensure that Canadian farmers have access to adequate sources of the long-term credit they need to finance their farm businesses. There are important clauses in the bill which will allow the Farm Credit Corporation to be more responsive to the needs of Canadian producers.
The serious problem of how to see that the family farm stays in the family has received much attention in recent years. This bill provides a solution to that problem. One of the amendments would allow the FCC to provide financing to a farming corporation to fund a shareholder loan in order to allow the entry of another individual into the farming operation. Sons and daughters will thus be able to join their parents on the family farm.
According to the present Farm Credit Act, the corporation can make loans only on the security of farm lands or farm lands and chattels. Additional security can be taken but a loan cannot be based on this additional security. An amendment in this bill would allow additional security, as defined in the regulations, to be taken into consideration in calculating the size of a loan that a borrower may take out. This additional security could be, for instance, an equity interest in feeder cattle or even savings certificates which, if cashed before maturity, would result in a loss.
Currently, the corporation is limited to maintaining accounts in its own name in the Bank of Canada or in chartered banks designated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. February 1, 1982

MacEachen). It is proposed that in the future the corporation, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, be allowed to maintain accounts in its own name in any bank or financial institution in or outside of Canada. This would greatly improve the cash management opportunities of the corporation as well as its Financial performance.
This bill also contains a provision to increase the number of members of the corporation's board from five to seven. It has had a five-person board since 1959. However, 22 years later, the business of the corporation has grown in complexity and scope. The addition of two members with their diverse experience would greatly enhance the work of the board.
There are a number of other measures in the bill which could be considered a housekeeping nature. They are, nevertheless, necessary to eliminate obsolete items, as well as to update the act to reflect current agricultural conditions. The result will be an act which is easier to understand and to administer.
The Farm Credit Corporation fulfils a vital function in helping both Canadian farmers finance their operations and in providing advisory services to them. Credit advisers provide counselling to all clients and potential clients at the early stages of their development plans. There are also borrowers who recognize that they face higher levels of risk and would benefit from continuous farm business analysis, financial planning and the production and financial monitoring that the advisory services program offers.
Of the total loans approved annually, more than 15 per cent of the recipients agree to the continuous advisory services program. What I find so interesting about this program is the definite progress shown by the farmers who participate. Let us not forget that the participants are generally of a higher risk category with lower equity and higher loan-to-security ratios. When they start with the program, borrowers learn to manage their resources with a definite goal in mind-to become successful farmers. With time, most accounts become successful. By the time that they are released from advisory services, their repayment record is comparable to those who were never on the program.
As for the lending program, the results of the FCC special farm survey showed beyond a doubt how valuable the corporation's contribution is to the agricultural industry.
The survey examined the financial characteristics of the people who have received funds from the Farm Credit Corporation in 1981 and compared them to the average Canadian farmer. It is clear the FCC is currently lending to a much smaller scale of farm than the average. On a national basis, the average assets of FCC borrowers in 1981 were $375,000 compared to $518,700 for the average Canadian farmer. At the same time, FCC farmer debts were $185,000 as opposed to $78,000 for the average period. This results in a net worth of 51 per cent for the FCC borrowers compared to 85 per cent for the average farmer.
This indicates that the FCC is assisting the lower half of the farmers in Canada and also suggests that not many of the
Farm Loans
farmers in the top one third level are receiving aid from the FCC. The survey is evidence that the Farm Credit Corporation is meeting its objective of assisting the smaller, beginning farmer.
Let me point out that the corporation accomplishes these functions without appropriations from Parliament and covers its cost of operation, including losses, on a 1 per cent margin. Especially laudatory is its patient collection policy on overdue accounts.
It has displayed in the years since it was founded sound management policies, but above all a sense of humanity. I hope hon. members will join with me in supporting this bill which will allow the Farm Credit Corporation to do an even better job for Canadian farmers.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be able to take part in this debate this afternoon. I have the honour of representing one of the major, if not the major, agricultural areas of British Columbia. Naturally, I am vitally interested in all aspects of this bill which deal with the agricultural community and its problems.
In introducing this measure for second reading, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) stated:
Madam Speaker, this legislation is extremely important to the farm community and to Canada as a whole. It proposes measures which will strengthen the role of the federal Farm Credit Corporation in helping Canadian farmers invest in their industry's future.
I appreciate the fact that the minister is interested in the cause of the agricultural industry. Of course, if he were not he would not be in the particular portfolio which he has. However, I think that we are in danger of restricting the application of policies to perhaps a relatively limited proportion of our population. After all, the population of the agricultural community is shrinking and therefore it seems as though it is destined, at least for the present time, to occupy a lesser position numerically than many other industries.
I say that we are inclined to look upon it as a measure to assist farmers, and I appreciate that fact, but I think we must broaden our vision and realize that this bill will not just help the farmers but will meet a worldwide need. 1 think that this will place a different perspective on this bill, rather than looking at it from purely an agricultural point of view. In actual fact, it is a matter of importance to approximately 24 million Canadians. It is also of vast importance to a great many people right around the world who will be looking to us in the future for their requirements as far as food products are concerned.
Although projected population figures vary considerably, it is generally agreed that the population increase will be very substantial in the future. In light of this there will be a greatly increased demand for agricultural products. It has been stated that in the eighties the scenario will be demand outstripping supply. We are told that world food supply has increased approximately 2 per cent over the last several years, while demand has risen at a rate of 3 per cent or 4 per cent. By 1990

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
the world's population is expected to increase to 5.25 billion from the 1980 level of 4.25 billion, and those with a seer's outlook state that by the year 2000 we could have a world population of about 7 billion people.
An article in Dun's Review of April, 1981, entitled "Enough Food for AH" refers to previous predictions of food shortages which failed to materialize but states:
Today, the spectre looms again. But, unlike the past, the subject is no longer confined to a debate among academics. The possibility of food shortages in the 1980s is being seriously addressed by farmers and economists, grain merchants and politicians, food company executives and commodity traders. Indeed, says University of Minnesota professor William Cochrane, who was the Agriculture Department's chief economist during the Kennedy-Johnson years: "For quite a while. I was a voice crying in the wilderness. But now quite a large portion of the agricultural analysts share my views that food shortages will occur during this decade."
Therefore, in view of these interesting facts it seems to me that we must give attention to the agricultural industry because in the final analysis we are making a contribution, as I have said, and must make a contribution not only to meet our own immediate needs but also to meet the needs of the world at large.
By that I am not implying that the answer to world food shortages is the massive transfer of produce only. The most important long-term solution in assisting many of the chronically underfed nations is to improve their own production capability, and in many instances this can be done in very unsophisticated ways. However, there will always remain a demand for food. Therefore, we talk about the Farm Credit Corporation and how we are going to assist farmers. According to figures presented with respect to suggested additional funds to be placed in the hands of the Farm Credit Corporation, under present circumstances only a little over 200 farmers will benefit. That will not go very far toward meeting the need of our agricultural community.
I suggest that the role of government is essentially to create an economic climate in which the private entrepreneur-that includes the farmer, of course-is able to function adequately in his own particular sphere of activity in the development and maintenance of a dynamic and productive economy. Unfortunately, while the minister says that he is endeavouring to assist farmers and is doing everything he possibly can to help them overcome present difficulties-I agree, and I believe he is trying-on the other hand government policies which tend to restrict activity, discourage initiative and penalize enterprise can only deepen resentment and despair and undermine the very foundations of our nation.
To many farmers today the question is whether they should continue to struggle on, in the face of the restricted impact of government policies, until the roof falls in, or should they quit, salvage what they can of their equity and apply their energies to other pursuits? This question was posed to me not too long ago by one of the farmers in my constituency. He was examining very carefully whether he would be able to deal with the crisis situation in which agriculture finds itself today and whether he would face it and fight it out or just close up shop and turn elsewhere to make a living. Today many are living on
the depreciation of their assets, and when that is exhausted, that will mean the Finish.
Farm income is tied in with this because when farm income is not adequate to meet needs and provide for the replacement of machinery and assets, then farmers certainly will not have any money left to expand their operations or to do whatever is necessary to fulfil their responsibilities to the common good.
I have an article taken from the Abbotsford, Sumas and Matsqui News, a paper published in my area. This article also appeared in some of the other papers in my constituency. The article states:
Canadian farmers can brace themselves for smaller "take-home pay" in 1982 ... and British Columbia is prophesied to take one of the largest percentage cuts.
Estimates released at the federal outlook conference in Ottawa are for realized net farm income in Canada to reach $3.4 billion in the coming year. That is 15 per cent lower than 1981's level which, in turn, was up 22 per cent from 1980.
Farmers will be faced with the same old cost-price squeeze. Their cash receipts are expected to climb about 4 per cent in 1982 to $19.2 billion. But their operating expenses and depreciation charges will more than eat up this slight gain. These costs are expected to grow about 10 per cent to $16.1 billion.
I will not put any more of that article on the record, but it does point out the difficulty farmers and other businessmen are facing. They have the problem not only of how to make a living but also of how to build up their operations in a way which will meet the challenges of the future and enable them to fulfil their responsibility in the field of agricultural production. I think this is something which ties in with the proposal we have before us today, which is to place more money in the hands of the Farm Credit Corporation.
One of the reasons we have to have more money and why there must be a greater contribution in this way to farm operations is that the farmer presently cannot build up a surplus in order to meet the needs of tomorrow. He is just living at the limit of his capacity and production at the present time. Why should this be? I suggest that there are too many obstacles in the way of achieving the very thing the minister is desirous of achieving, and that is to assist farmers, through additional financing, to carry on their operations and also to expand in order to meet the needs. One of the reasons this is necessary is that government policies, and particularly those contained in the recent budget, are counterproductive as far as farm income is concerned. We are lending farmers money yet extracting taxes from them beyond their ability to pay. 1 think one of the reasons for this is that they are still tied to high interest rates. Perhaps they could have got by if they were still able to borrow money at 10 per cent or 11 per cent but in recent times, when faced with interest rates of 20 per cent, 21 per cent or 22 per cent, they could not accomplish their objectives and pay their way.
The high incidence of forced sales, foreclosures and bankruptcies in the agricultural sector is a sad reflection on a nation such as ours. It is an indictment of a government policy that does not meet the needs of an important sector of our economy.
February 1, 1982

On May 5, 1981, before the exorbitant increase in the cost of money, the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture addressed Members of Parliament as follows:
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is most concerned about the increasing number of actual farm bankruptcies and foreclosures. The evidence is that there is a rising flood of farmers in trouble, and bank interest rates are the crushing blow that will put them under. If this is not so, a federal emergency program will get at the truth and no harm done.
Farmers in this position who have nowhere to go for help must have some program which will give them a chance for survival. Failure by the federal government to act and act quickly on this matter would be simply irresponsible.
The minister states that he has been introducing legislation and has outlined various proposals made in order to assist farmers in this particular situation so that they will be able to carry on and function as operating farmers. When we have raised this question in the House he has referred to the Small Business Development Bond, but the qualifications required for that program are so restrictive that very few farmers are able to benefit from it. Even those who, to use the words of the minister, "need it most" have been unable to obtain any help when they are in dire straits. Many farmers who have applied to the Farm Credit Corporation have met with a response similar to the one they received when they applied for the development bond-that there was no money left. There was no money available under the Small Business Development Bond program, there is no money from the Farm Credit Corporation, there is no money anywhere.
I think this points very dramatically to the failure of the Farm Credit Corporation to meet the needs of the farm community. The result is evident in the increased numbers of forced sales, foreclosures and bankruptcies. These numbers are already on the record so I shall not repeat them.
The minister's rather pathetic confession was reported in the Valley Magazine of Wednesday, February 25, 1981 in an article which began as follows:
If you're a farmer with a credit problem, federal agriculture minister Eugene Whelan says he'd truly like to help . . . but there may not be all that much he can do.
Later the article stated:
But even at the national level there is only a limited amount we can do because it is a world problem. The fact is that Canada's success in holding down inflation has been so much better than many other countries is a tribute to the hard work and productivity of Canadian industry, as well as to our rich endowment of natural resources, including our agricultural land.
So the minister confessed that there was not very much he could do to assist farmers in their plight.
The recent federal budget which was supposed to be based on the principle of fairness, equity and justice is proving just the opposite, not only as it relates to the agricultural sector but to practically every sector of the economy. In an article which appeared in the Chilliwack Progress in my constituency, an accountant used the phrase "kick 'em while they're down" to describe the budget that was brought in. He was referring to the agricultural community and went on to point out a great number of the adverse features of the budget. The equity in a family farm for retirement has been eroded. Higher down payments will be required on the sale of farms and this will, in
Farm Loans
turn, reduce the number of potential purchasers which would no doubt have an effect on the price. The higher down payments will prevent young people from getting into agriculture. If the problems facing farmers were bad yesterday, they are compounded tremendously for the future.
There are many other things that work against the farmer's effort to pay his own way, to build up his equity, to get along under his own steam, as it were, without relying on the contributions or loans of the federal government. I do not think farmers want to borrow money for the sake of borrowing; they do it because they have to.
I wish to refer now to the matter of capital gains on farm sales which have a very serious effect on the agricultural community. As has been pointed out in debates in this House, promises have been made relative to legislation dealing with this subject but we, and the farmers of Canada, are still waiting for it. When are we going to see the update of the valuation day values to meet the demands of justice and decency? Why will the government not accept the common sense and valid position of this party that would permit a once-in-a-lifetime exemption from capital gains on the sale of a farm?
Some people may think I am getting a little far from the subject of the Farm Credit Corporation, but this is all tied in together. It is because of all these things that we need organizations such as the Farm Credit Corporation. I had other things to say on this question but 1 will not take the time of the House to deal with them now.
Perhaps I could do no better than put on the record a statement issued by the chairman of our caucus and the spokesman for this party on agriculture. In a news release dated January 28, 1982, issued by the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), and the spokesman for agriculture for our party, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), it was stated:
Finally, after three years of waiting, the government introduced Bill C-88 in the House of Commons on January 27. This bill will allow the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow supplemental funding from the private marketplace.
Last year Agriculture Minister Whelan held out the promise that this bill and the budget would help farmers overcome their financial difficulties. This was another empty promise on the part of Mr. Whelan.
The budget produced more pain than help because it detrimentally changed the capital gains tax reserve and eliminated the Income-Averaging Annuity Contracts and the Small Business Development Bond program for expansion purposes. Although the budget also gave the FCC $50 million, this was a far cry from its real needs estimated to be from $500 million to $1 billion.
When we look at an additional $50 million, in light of the adverse effect of government policies on the agricultural community and the fact that the government is making it impossible for farmers to carry on their operations in a desired manner, it seems to be almost a slap in the face. When farmers have gone to the Farm Credit Corporation they were told, "Sorry, we have no money". The corporation ran out of money a long time ago, but now the government suggests that it will put in another $50 million. This is a far cry from what is actually needed in order to make money available to farmers

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
who require it for survival, let alone those who require it for expansion in order to meet the increased needs of a world community which will be faced with food shortages in the near future.
The press release goes on:
Bill C-88 will not provide any needed short-term relief. Even with the extra $50 million, the Farm Credit Corporation has virtually run out of money to lend. It needs more funds.
Bill C-88 should be an important and worth-while measure in the long-range funding of the Farm Credit Corporation and, as a result, we will support it provided the government gives a firm commitment that its direct funding to the FCC will not be cut back. We also hope that the government will guarantee the bonds floated by the FCC so that they could be sold more quickly.
The real tragedy is that this bill has been introduced three years too late. If it had been in place last year, the 261 Canadian farmers who had been forced into bankruptcy might still be productive farmers today, let alone the untold hundreds more who were forced out of business through foreclosure and forced sale.
In closing, I am not saying that the Farm Credit Corporation has not done the job given to it, considering the amount of money made available to it. It was not the fault of the FCC. It comes down to a matter of the government's unrealistic attitudes toward the farming community, its tremendous contribution to our nation today and the contribution it will make in the future to all those people who will be affected by the shortage of food which we are led to anticipate in days ahead. I trust the government will accept some of these suggestions.
I hope it will not only provide additional funds but will take a look at what has been done to farmers by federal government policy which made it necessary for them to turn, in such a great measure, to the Farm Credit Corporation and other lending institutions in order to succeed in their chosen vocation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I welcome the opportunity to address the House on Bill C-88, to amend the Farm Credit Act. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has been present in the House, but I am sorry he had to leave to attend a cabinet committee meeting. I had hoped that some of my remarks would evoke a response from him. ifhe minister has been vocal and has said much in public respecting his views of the interests of farmers and the action that Parliament, and government in particular, should take to assist farmers. We find that in growing numbers farmers are coming under more and more pressure with respect to carrying on their operations. The parliamentary secretary is present and 1 am sure he will make detailed notes of what I say and take them to the minister, so that he will have the benefit of some of the advice 1 want to give him.
We should look back over the last few months to find out exactly what the minister said concerning the plight of Canadians farmers. I have one or two copies of press clippings which by and large are correct quotations of the minister. Certainly the minister has not taken it upon himself to challenge the accuracy of any of these quotations. He has been more than vocal. He has been pounding his chest in public, speaking on behalf of Canadian farmers and threatening dire consequences if certain actions were not taken by the government. A headline appeared in the October 11 edition of The
Toronto Sun entitled "Whelan: 'Get off your butts'." I want to make a direct quotation of the minister, directed to Canadian farmers. He warned farmers and blamed Canadian banks for the woes of farmers. He said that there should be a temporary halt to farm foreclosures. Also he said that the banks were at fault for letting farmers take out huge demand floating loans which they could not afford. As reported in the article, he said:
I used to have a farm and I was a farm leader. I didn't just holler criticism, but made constructive suggestions ... I don't want to stay on as Minister of Agriculture if some new program isn't instituted. I'm an honest broker as far as politicians go.
As reported in The Windsor Star of October 10, 1981, the Minister of Agriculture was in full flight, oratorically speaking; the moon must have been in a certain position. This man was forging ahead on behalf of farmers. We were waiting with bated breath to see what would happen as soon as the minister returned to Ottawa. He met with his cabinet colleagues and told them the facts of life, how farmers across the country were suffering. As reported in The Windsor Star under the headline entitled "Gene: Wait and see what budget brings," Dave Pink, Star agriculture reporter, referred to Essex, which is the minister's home area. The article read:
Agriculture Minister Gene Whelan says he's expecting help for financially troubled farmers in the new federal government budget.
And if that help doesn't come, Whelan has said he's ready to resign from the cabinet.
"Gene Whelan has been a backbencher before," he said in a Friday night interview.
"I'm very concerned about my position as an honest broker in politics. You can only go so far," Whelan later told a gathering of Essex Windsor Liberals. "We've had meetings. We've made our submissions. We will wait and sec what action the budget takes in the not too distant future."
The farmers of Canada, as one, stood and knelt by their bedsteads that night thinking that the Minister of Agriculture would take action and in fact do something to relieve the enormous economic consequences which they have suffered over the course of past years-unprecedented interest rates and costs of production rising almost daily.
The budget came down. As every farmer or anyone who has had a chance to read the budget knows, it contained virtually nothing for Canadian farmers. It was a disgrace. There was nothing for the average farmer. There was nothing to give any hope with respect to the economic circumstances faced by Canadian farmers today. What do we have? We have the same Minister of Agriculture. There has been no resignation. Interest rates remain high.
The Minister of Agriculture has now decided that rather than resigning he will change his tune slightly. Now the attack is on the banks. He talked about a "verge on fraud" in the banks' treatment of farmers, as reported in the January 14, 1982, edition of The Globe and Mail. What exactly does the minister mean by verging on fraud? He should give us some details so that we can change the legislation and do something to help farmers against the fraud which is being perpetrated upon them by banks. The minister is silent, he says nothing; he said, "I cannot speak". On an opposition day last week a
February 1, 1982

motion was put forward, at which time the minister had an opportunity to rise and show where he stood with respect to banks. He stood with the government, in opposition to the opposition motion. This is the background of the Minister of Agriculture coming forward with this legislation as a solution to the problems of Canadian farmers.
What farmer or what Canadian can hold up the minister as a credible representative in cabinet of their interests? Surely this is a case where the minister's bark is far worse than his bite. There is no meaningful help for farmers, either in the budget or in any piece of legislation. He stands on the public stage humiliated and unable to get his way on behalf of farmers across Canada. 1 say that the honourable thing for the minister to do is to resign. Whatever happened to that old tradition, when a question of principle arose, of ministerial responsibility? Whatever happened to the concept of a minister saying "I have had enough, I am resigning; 1 said I would resign and I am resigning". As far as this government is concerned, that principle has gone by the by.
The answer which the minister brings forward with respect to the agricultural policy that he has for Canadian farmers is Bill C-88. This is a very important piece of legislation. It is far-seeing and will help every farmer across our nation. This legislation will enable the number of directors on the board of directors of the Farm Credit Corporation to be increased from five to seven members. Every farmer in Canada will applaud this progressive move on their behalf.
This bill contains a provision-
-(a) to remove the present thirty-five year age limitation for loans under section 33.
This is a brave minister!
This bill also updates some of the language in the Farm Credit Act. Every farmer is waiting for this to be done. I have letters by the carload asking when the language of the Farm Credit Act is to be updated.
You have heard from our colleagues, Mr. Speaker. Naturally we support the principle and thrust of this bill. But when we speak on this bill, we have to point out to the minister that something more is required. Surely this is not the response the government has to assist farmers out of the difficult times which they face in Canada today. We all have to look at the lack of economic support for our farming community in general that is being evidenced by the policies of this government. We see a disturbing trend on the part of this government to sabotage the economic viability of the small family-based farms. They are the backbone of my province and of Canadian agriculture and rural life. There are policies against farmers maintaining the family farm.
1 want to point out to hon. members that in the west there are 150,000 producers. The families of these producers are directly engaged in the production of grain which is largely for export. At present $4 billion worth of grain is exported annually. This has a multiplier effect of four on the Canadian economy. In terms of economic benefit, there is no industry
Farm Loans
that produces more economic spin-off, stability and potential gains for our economy.
Some of the other sectors of the farm economy, such as the dairy sector, the poultry sector and the red meat sector, make a significant contribution to the over-all wellbeing of the Canadian economy. Canadian farmers have very special financial needs. Almost all independent farmers are dependent upon credit. They borrow in order to operate. General operating costs are fixed and unavoidable. Energy costs, machinery and other capital costs have skyrocketed. A farmer cannot rationally starve his livestock and ruin his land in order to cut costs.
Farmers are among the most seriously affected by a policy of high interest rates. This policy means that farm turnovers are made that much more difficult for young people who are attempting to get into farming. They simply cannot afford the additional interest expense. We see the average age of owners of farm land reaching 50 in 1982. Many farmers hold on to their land long past their age of retirement. They do this because the party to whom they wish to sell, very often a son or a daughter, cannot arrange the purchase financing or cannot afford it.
Obviously there is a major role for a corporation, such as the Farm Credit Corporation, to provide reasonable amounts of funding at reasonable rates. For an industry that provides so much to the Canadian economy, this is absolutely essential.
As my colleague who spoke before me has pointed out, there has been considerable delay in bringing forward this bill. In the process the Farm Credit Corporation has become cash starved. We in this party understand the importance and necessity of raising the limits on capital and providing for a corresponding increase in the corporation's borrowing capacity. We also welcome the new flexibility of being able to borrow in the market. As my colleagues have pointed out, we have taken a position of concern because this new direction may lead to a cut in direct funding of the Farm Credit Corporation.
I am waiting to hear from the minister with respect to a commitment by this government that such a cut in that sort of direct funding will not occur.
The industry is also cash starved at this time. This government in its budget has made only a token effort to come up with assistance. Our party has called for additional short-term funding for the Farm Credit Corporation of $500 million. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture says that agriculture needs $1 billion injected into it immediately. People who are involved in the day to day operations of farms through their organizations indicate that is the kind of money that is needed at the present time to be injected into the farming industry.
This government saw fit to allocate only something in the vincinity of $50 million through the Farm Credit Corporation. This is an amount conceivably only enough to deal with as few as 225 applications for assistance, to take the maximum number in that particular hypothesis.
What else does the government give us aside from this additional money for the Farm Credit Corporation? There was, of course, reference to the Small Business Development

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
Bond. What should have been a useful tool for long-term capital investment is now only available to those having serious cash flow problems.
Stories have been coming in about the difficulties that small businesses and farmers have had in convincing banks to extend any financing arrangements through the Small Business Development Bond. I simply ask the question whether hon. members have had any experience in this area. You have had experience in the private sector, Mr. Speaker, I know that, but I have yet to meet a lending agency, regardless of advertising, where money is available only on the signature of the borrower, whatever the particular sensitivity of the local manager may be. If someone is in so-called dire straits and approaches a bank for a loan, that person will not be greeted with open arms.
The federal government has restricted the loans in these instances to those in dire straits and financial difficulty. But the government has not said to the banks that if anything goes wrong the government will set up a guarantee that they will not lose all of this money. The banks will look at every application they receive on the basis that money lent must be recovered in the interest of maintaining the viability of their operation. It will be very difficult for those farmers in dire straits.
This government has created in this budget a further hindrance to transfer land by removing the income-averaging annuity contract. Even with the transitional rules announced on December 18, the purchase is vendor financed. The vendor may very well have to borrow to pay his or her taxes after the reserve period lapses. This again puts an impediment in the way of young farmers who want to get into the business and in the way of older farmers and land owners who want to get out. So, Mr. Speaker, we see the government offering only token support to farmers in additional farm credit funding in the budget while at the same time limiting the effectiveness of the Small Business Development Bond and the IAAC.
The farming industry in Canada, particularly in Saskatchewan, is going through all sorts of difficulties. Land prices have increased dramatically in recent years, as have operating costs. It seems the government could do far more to lessen the pressure on the industry at this critical time. The final irony is to watch a Minister of Agriculture who protests so loud and long about his love for the farming community, and then in the same breath allows the FCC rate of borrowing to go up to 16% per cent.
It is fascinating to listen to his criticism of the banks. On January 28 last he made one of his usual verbal outbursts on the subject when he said:
Why can the farmers not borrow from their local banks or credit unions, as 1 might if I were buying a new home or seeking funds to start a new business? Why, indeed? One need only look at the record of the banks over the last five years as to how they have handled, or maybe I should say mishandled, farm loans to know the answer to that question.
It is utterly hypocritcal, Mr. Speaker, for the minister to continue his tirade against the banks when he stands with a government which cares so little for the economic needs of the country's farmers. If the government wanted to make a decent commitment to farmers, why did it put only $50 million into the FCC in additional funds? It needed ten times that amount. Why does it put up the FCC lending rate if it has such great sympathy for the farmer? Why did it assault the farmer's pocketbook in the budget? Little wonder, Mr. Speaker, that farmers do not bother listening to the minister any more; he simply does not deliver.
It is said in western Canada that the bones of long dead western Liberals are becoming archaeological treasures. A museum in Regina has a lot of these old bones and they have a new category. We have Tyrannosaurus Rex, Brontosaurus, and now we are getting the rare "liberalus defunctus".
