The "twin from Saskatoon East" is in the House as usual. I am saying these things so that he will take notes and go back to that Liberal rally in Saskatoon East held in the nearest phone booth and tell all the Liberals in Saskatchewan exactly what should be done on behalf of western farmers. If you take notes he may do some good, instead of making these interjections.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the farmers of my province have been subjected to massive pressures in the last ten years. Operating expenses have risen from $966 million in 1976 to $1.58 billion in 1980, a 63.6 per cent increase. In that same time interest payments paid by farmers have increased by 117 per cent. However, the farmers' income has certainly not kept pace. Farmers also have great difficulties in transferring land due to the imposition of a capital gains tax. They are taxed on a gain not of their making, one that is often artificially inflated due to speculation.
The November 12 budget contributed absolutely nothing to the resolution of their problems. It contained minimal financial help, further complicated land transfers and disabled the useful aspects of the small business development bond. Many of you will remember the display of support for the farming community in the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). Under that budget a farmer would have been able to roll over up to $200,000 of a taxable capital gain on the sale of farm land into an RRSP. That was certainly a more fair and effective way of allowing farmers to plan for their retirement. This outfit, this Liberal government, seems to think there is something wrong with a person spending his or her working years buying and farming land, selling it and then enjoying a productive retirement on the proceeds.
With the proper service guarantee and a clear commitment by the government to provide the appropriate subsidy, longterm planning can be made by the transportation industry, government and farmers alike, in western Canada particularly.
There have been suggestions recently that an announcement will be made shortly with respect to the Crow rate in western
February 1, 1982

Canada. Some of these statements indicated an early decision by the government on this rate. This all affects the viability and stability of the grain farming industry in western Canada.
I simply advise the Minister of Agriculture, as he is involved in these decisions, to heed the words of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall:
once tampering with the statutory rate is accepted or condoned as an item on the bargaining table, all will be lost. For once the subject is on the bargaining table, it will only be a matter of time until it is lost step by step. There is no position to take except to adhere through thick and thin that the Crow rate is not bargainable.
I make those remarks with respect to another initiative announced by this government, and to take a look at what in fact may be the scenario western Canada is facing with respect to another program announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), among others. This is because, in my view, a decision on the Crow goes hand in hand with the appearance of the western development fund.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the $4 billion elusive dream of the October 28, 1980, budget is now a $1.3 billion nightmare for westerners. It was purportedly a fund to modernize the grain handling and transportation sectors, as well as promote western industrial diversification. In the last budget it was slashed by 60 per cent, which turns it into a complete sham. A portion of this year's allocation of $148 million is to be used to assist Vancouver in the purchase of urban light rapid transit. I point out, Mr. Speaker, that all this equipment comes from central Canada. So much for providing jobs, secondary industry and technology to the west.
I wish the minister was here because he indicated some incredulity with respect to this statement which was confirmed by officials in the Department of Finance. Out of this fund the sum of $81 million has been funnelled to Canadian farmers for losses sustained because of the Soviet grain embargo. Now, Mr. Speaker, western farmers are entitled to recover their losses from that embargo. However, this government is paying them from a fund declared to be for the economic development of the west. I should add that $13 million of that payment goes to farmers in Ontario and Quebec.
It is my submission that any payments for compensation to western farmers should have come out of the general treasury. For the government to pay those moneys out of the western development fund is a complete betrayal of the promises made to western Canada.
What about the rest of the western development fund? I fear that a much greater problem faces us. No plans have yet been announced specifically for the rest of that money. However, would it not be convenient for the government simply to remove the statutory freight rate and then have this new fund waiting to pay off farmers? The Liberals, of course, would be most anxious to point out that all this money is to be used to improve western transportation. Of course, the fallacy of that argument is that the railways are already partially compensated for losses sustained as a result of the Crow. Therefore, in
Farm Loans
actual fact, no new money will be put into the west. It will just be old money in new packages.
To let the Liberals get away with this sleight of hand will be an open door to the complete erosion of the benefits farmers have obtained because of the Crow rate. Maybe next year the fund will be slashed again and, all of a sudden, farmers will be paying the full cost of moving grain with no compensation. Therefore, I simply put the warning out to all hon. members of the House that the future shape of the agricultural economy hangs in the balance.
The problem is that if this money is simply paid out as part of the settlement of the Crow, it will not be used for its declared purpose of placing seed money in western Canada for industrial and transportation research and development. These crucial needs of the west are being ignored to the serious detriment of our farming community. I say to hon. members that the indecision on the part of the federal government in developing a rational, global transportation policy in the west causes much uncertainty, many lost opportunities, and ultimately affects the income of our western farmers. This so-called western development fund is a case in point, because it is unfortunate that this fund appears to be ending up simply as a Liberal slush fund to be administered in the usual ad hoc and arbitrary manner without the benefit of appropriate public input and debate.
If the minister were here, I would also point out that there are other initiatives which are needed in terms of the western farmer, aside from the budgetary assistance which can be rendered. An atmosphere could be created in western Canada to let young people know that farming is a career which will be productive and satisfying, and will bring in reasonable returns. There must be a general atmosphere of taxation policy and policy with respect to retiring funds so that people will know that a very productive, important and integral part of our society, the agricultural sector, will remain viable.
In this context I want to make only a few other references to another initiative I think the government should take. I think agricultural research must be stepped up across our country. Various projects are crying out for funding. There has been reticence, and pressure has been put upon the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts), who has spoken about making new commitments with respect to research and development in our country. Again, I hate to sound immodest, but I say to the minister that it would do himself a lot of good if he simply looked back at some of the initiatives taken by my government concerning that particular area of policy.
In my city of Saskatoon, the veterinary infectious diseases organization is doing excellent work. An example of the research work being done is the development of a vaccine to combat the most common form of calf scours, a vaccine which took four years to develop. More money is now needed to develop vaccine to be given to young calves to prevent shipping fever. Another vaccine is needed to control mud fever in turkeys, which costs the Canadian turkey industry some $9

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
million annually, and another for the prevention of the spread of respiratory diseases in young pigs for the pork industry.
Major research is also required in the grain and oil seed industries. The ironic aspect here, as pointed out many times by my colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), is that a portion of the funding needed for this research could be derived from funds left over from the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Some $9 million remains from that check-off fund. It now sits in a non-interest bearing account while it could be used by researchers, on behalf of farmers, for very productive research projects. I congratulate the hon. member for Moose Jaw on his private member's bill which would make this a reality. For some reason which is hard for me to understand, that very reasonable, thoughtful proposition put forward by the hon. member for Moose Jaw has been resisted by the Minister of Agriculture. One would have thought that a minister, who has received headlines for his statements of support for farmers across this country, would have been in line to have said to my colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw, "That is a good, constructive suggestion; let us get on with the job. Let us put this money to work. Let us not keep it in the general treasury, where it is bearing no interest for the benefit of the people who, in fact, have invested this money in the prairie farm assistance program."
I think there is one last issue which affects many farmers in western Canada, and I want to make brief reference to it. It is a question which is being asked with respect to the Wheat Board and the contract which it has carried on, in fact, for the benefit of farmers. The projections by Saskatchewan agriculturalists forecast a final payment for durum which was in the area of $1.10 per bushel. The final payment was, in fact, 1.6 cents a bushel. Contract prices are not published. In light of projections, we must ask why such a shortfall took place this year. Why are we not able to get some information with respect to the basis upon which that payment was made? Many farmers want the Wheat Board to be more forthcoming with respect to the basis upon which that calculation was made.
I want to summarize my remarks concerning this bill. Its objective to free the Farm Credit Corporation to go into the marketplace to obtain funds needed to supply the requests for money by the farmers of this country is something we support, as indicated on different occasions by hon. members from our party who have spoken previously. However, in light of this government's lack of support for the farming community in the budget and its indecisiveness in dealing with the transportation of farm products, and considering the way things have been going over the last few years with this outfit, we seriously wonder whether this will not be used by the government to cut direct funding to the Farm Credit Corporation.
Farmers of this country have very special credit needs and operate on a very slim profit margin, particularly in these tough times, and this is not evident anywhere as much as it is in the west. The increases in operating and capital costs have not been of their own making. They need the support and encouragement of the government. The budget gives little
tangible support and, in reality, causes hardships for many who are undergoing transfers, a process which is essential to keep youth in the industry and enable older farmers to provide for themselves during their retirement. Lack of a transportation policy causes long-term uncertainty and loss of income to farmers.
Therefore, I say to the Minister of Agriculture, "Be as good as your word." Speeches filled with the rhetoric for which the minister is famous are not sufficient; some action is now required. We take no partisan pride in standing here to tell the minister that he has miserably failed, as his government has failed, to help the farmers in Canada. I would just as soon stand up and compliment the minister, and to say, "Job well done! You have spoken out and taken action." As a member of the opposition, it gives me no pleasure to be critical; but if one lives in my district, one knows the problems of farmers. Over the course of the last recess, farmers came into my office to say that their own personal circumstances are such that they are experiencing a sense of uncertainty, that they do not know where they are going. I have received tragic letters. I think that if hon. members lived in my area, they would be standing, as I am now standing, to say, on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture, that words are fine, but action is better.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to speak on the Farm Credit Act amendments before the House today, Bill C-88. It is significant that during the past week we have been dealing with two important pieces of legislation. Last week we dealt with the Canagrex bill which will play a major role in the future in the marketing of farm products overseas. It will expand that role, working with the private sector, the agricultural community, co-operatives, marketing agents and boards to increase our sales overseas. Someone described the decade of the eighties to be the decade of food and agricultural production, just as energy was our top priority during the seventies. It is therefore significant that we are dealing immediately after the Christmas recess with these two important pieces of legislation.
There is no doubt that the Canadian agricultural industry requires additional assistance. It is an industry that extends across the country, mainly with small family farm businesses working at a time when farm input costs are rising rapidly. The cost of land during the past decade has been rapidly rising. The difficulties of young people getting involved in agriculture have increased tremendously. Added to this is the uncertainty of climate, money and world prices, making it very difficult for an uncertain industry, to say the least.
The important thing about the Farm Credit Corporation is that it brings stability to the lending institutions. There is the provision for long-term lending. During the past 12 months there have been tremendous problems in borrowing from the banks, which have a floating interest rate. The total uncertainty of that situation is just impossible for many farm operations to cope with.
February 1, 1982

It is significant that 70 per cent of loans made by the Farm Credit Corporation are to younger farmers who do not have the established track record that older, more experienced and more knowledgeable operators often have. The Farm Credit Corporation must continue to provide such interest and concern for young people wanting to get into agriculture. It is important that we have an agency like the Farm Credit Corporation which has a certain amount of flexibility. When unforeseen problems arise, especially for young farmers, they should be able to defer payments for short periods of time. That sort of assistance is available.
The staff of the Farm Credit Corporation offices does a very good job. In almost every instance it assists young farmers in particular with counselling and advises them on financial matters. It assists them in putting together an economical and viable unit.
We are not dealing with small amounts of money. Let us look at the farm capital investment reported in the national census carried out in 1971. On average, the estimated value of a farm was $79,000. By 1976 this had risen to $190,000 and by 1980, according to the national census figures on the value of farm property, it had increased to $340,000. Therefore, we are dealing with very large amounts of money.
I compliment the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on being able to get this important piece of legislation to the House. I also compliment him on establishing the Anderson commission on August 28 to prepare a report on marketing and other aspects of the beef industry. Of all the farm industries which have had a difficult time during the past two years, the beef production industry has perhaps had a more difficult time than any other sector of our agricultural community.
If we look at the 1979 fall sales, the upper average price for calves selling in the Algoma-Manitoulin district was $1 to $1.10 a pound, sometimes as high as $1.15. In 1981 the average dropped to 70 cents a pound, with top loads as high as 75 cents. In any event, we are looking at an almost 30 per cent decrease in returns. I do not think any other sector of our economy has had to take a 30 per cent drop in revenue during the two-year period from the fall of 1979 to the fall of 1981.
Looking at the input side, the cost of fuel, fertilizer, money and so on has increased by at least 30 per cent. Between September, 1976, and September, 1981, gasoline costs increased by 74 per cent, diesel fuel by 84 per cent, fertilizer by 47 per cent and bank interest rates by as much as 80 per cent. These figures were put together by the Manitoulin beef producers organization.
Looking at the price of beef calves going on to the market in the fall, we see that the consumer buying red beef in the store has noticed a considerable increase, perhaps by as much as $1 a pound over the period of time from 1979 to 1981. Therefore, the consumer has not benefited. At the same time the beef producer has taken a terrific drop in gross revenue and has shown practically no profit for his time, effort, investment and enterprise.
Farm Loans
It is important that we place a very high priority on this farm legislation at this time. Input costs, funding and financing are terribly important and require the earnest consideration of this House and this government. If we look at the support offered by practically every other nation in the world, we see they provide preferential rates for borrowing, many well below 10 per cent and some as low as a zero interest rate. The legislation before us will enable the Minister of Agriculture and the Farm Credit Corporation to go outside of the conventional method of receiving all funding from the federal government, and borrow on the private market.
It seems to me that we should be looking at the possibility of assisting both young farmers who are going into business and retiring farmers by providing a means of funding. Both the retiring farmers and the young farmers starting up can take advantage of this new capacity of the Farm Credit Corporation to go outside the federal government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to secure its funding.
Another very important part of this bill is the measure for increased capitalization of the Farm Credit Corporation from $150 million to $255 million. This will allow the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow up to approximately $5.6 billion. This reflects the increased amount of borrowing which will be required. It also reflects the increased value of farm property over the last few years.
It is interesting to note that in 1975 the amount of borrowing was approximately $655 million. In 1980 it was up to approximately $2 billion, an increase of at least 20 per cent. I might also note that this legislation provides that the upper loan limits may be increased by regulation or by order in council. It is my understanding that it is proposed to increase the borrowing limits from $200,000 to $300,000 for a single applicant and from $400,000 to $500,000 for more than one applicant.
Also, I note that the legislation which the minister has introduced will remove the age limit of 35 years for people who will be phasing into farming, that is, will be working part-time at another job but will phase in over a five-year period. Removal of that over-35-years age limit is a worth-while change.
Along with the Canagrex bill and the Farm Credit Act amendments, which I hope the opposition will support, I hope the minister will move on rapidly to implement the report which is being prepared by the Anderson-Vandermeulen commission which he appointed last August.
During this past weekend I had an opportunity to travel with Mr. E. H. Anderson, who is serving on that commission, to meet with the livestock and beef producers in the Algoma and Manitoulin districts and hear of the difficult problems which they are facing. I had the opportunity to hear him respond to the kinds of representations he has been receiving across the country about the possibility of reconciling the vast number of stabilization programs which exist at the provincial

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
level and to hear proposals for the control of unlimited imports of red beef into our country from offshore areas.
I believe we must proceed in a deliberate, decisive but careful manner as soon as that commission report is given to the minister. If we do not take steps to ensure that we have a viable beef producing industry in Canada, we will end up with a few large producers and a few hobby farmers producing our beef. The present system of stabilization and marketing is totally inadequate, while at the same time-consumer prices continue to rise even though the returns to this vital industry have fallen dramatically over the last two years.
I am hopeful that the Farm Credit Act amendments will pass and increase the capacity of the corporation to secure funds at lower rates. I think the rates which were provided in the special legislation which was introduced in the budget, providing rates at 113A per cent, would be the direction interest rates would take under the legislation. I believe this bill provides some of the legislative framework for those special rates and will be useful in implementing them.
At the same time, the Small Business Development Bond which was introduced in the fall, to be available to agricultural producers who are not incorporated businesses, has been a useful tool. Of course, the Farm Credit Corporation legislation itself is the most desirable vehicle because of its long-term fixed rate of interest, there is counselling available, there is flexibility in it and it is especially valuable and more available to young farmers. At the same time, it provides a long-term credit plan to let agricultural producers know what the interest rate will be.
I hope that this legislation which will be beneficial to the vital farming industry, along with the other beneficial pieces of legislation which will be introduced in this session, will receive the support of the House.

subtopic: FARM CREDIT ACT FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to the amendments to the Farm Credit Act presented in Bill C-88.
I represent a sizeable community of farmers, many of whom have some financial problems, many others who are in desperate financial straits. These farmers and indeed all Canadian farmers have waited almost five years for changes to the Farm Credit Act to find their way from the minister's office to the House. That is a long time, especially for changes as general as those proposed in this bill.
1 see nothing in the bill representing major changes either to the Farm Credit Corporation or to the government's over-all agricultural policy. Given the five-year wait, 1 doubt if many farmers will accept the minister's latest excuse for delay, that he was waiting to hear from the Ontario Federation of Agriculture before he introduced the amendments to the Farm Credit Act. In fact, it appears that the minister has paid little heed to the wishes of Canadian farmers in drafting much of this bill. It is true that more money will be available to borrowers and that age discrimination criteria for receiving a loan will be lifted, but on important questions such as the capital pool of the Farm Credit Corporation and the level of interest rates on loans from the agency, there is little or
nothing at all in the changes that respond to the requests of farmers.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture requested early last year an increase of some $150 million for the Farm Credit Corporation to respond to the crisis in farm financing. What did they get? For many months they got nothing. In the November budget they finally got $45 million plus an additional $5 million to subsidize interest rates for approximately two years. That is one third of what they asked for.
The minister says that he listens. He does not listen very well. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture also said that interest rates of 14 per cent are all that farmers can afford to pay. But there is nothing spelled out in this bill to suggest measures will be adopted to reduce interest charged on farm credit loans from the current rate of 16.75 per cent.
I agree with my colleague, the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), when he characterizes the real problem of farm credit as not simply a problem of inadequate credit but one of net income being too low to pay the bills and maintain a viable operation. In Manitoba the realized net income of farmers actually decreased 42 per cent from 1975 to 1981. We all know, of course, that the cost of living did not decline with it. In fact, it increased by 88 per cent. To make up the shortfall in their net income or to undertake the expansion the minister suggested last week was necessary to achieve economies of scale for new technology, farmers have had to borrow at an increasing rate. In 1981 Manitoba farmers paid out $201 million in loan payments, an increase of some 359 per cent since 1975.
The agricultural policies of this government are forcing farmers further and further into debt. Last week the minister told this House that the Farm Credit Corporation is helping to ensure that the Canadian family farm remains a stable and viable entity. Perhaps the agency has helped some family farms, but has it not also been hindered in its ability to help make the family farm viable and stable?
In 1975, 72 per cent of all long-term credit taken out by farmers came from the Farm Credit Corporation. By 1979 the proportion had shrunk to 35 per cent. Who is responsible for that? Surely not the farmers. 1 doubt that there are many Canadian farmers who, on principle, would refuse to borrow at a lower rate from a government agency like the Farm Credit Corporation. It is this government that is responsible. It is responsible for the decline and the fall of the Farm Credit Corporation. With its tight purse strings it has hamstrung the agency. It has prevented it from keeping up with the increasing demand for farm credit. This government has stood in the way of the Farm Credit Corporation and prevented it from responding readily to the credit needs of Canadian farmers, and it has offered the banks-with their exorbitant interest rates and their $1.7 billion in profits-a bigger piece of the Farm Credit Act on a silver platter.
The crisis in farm financing and the declining role of the Farm Credit Corporation have been disastrous for Canadian
February 1, 1982

farmers. Last year 261 farms in Canada were forced into bankruptcy. That is more than twice as many farm bankruptcies as in 1979. An increase in farm bankruptcies of more than 100 per cent in two years is shocking.
1 mentioned a moment ago the dismal income situation faced by farmers today. When we see farmers' net income actually decrease over a period of seven years while the cost of everything else has increased, I do not think there is any reason to believe this increase in farm bankruptcies is in some way due to an increase in poor farm management. Farmers are doing their best to run stable and viable operations, but when their income is falling and their costs are increasing, they are forced to borrow. When the interest charges on the money they have had to borrow outstrip their earning potential, some of them are forced to declare bankruptcy. They are forced to give up their family farms.
Everyone should see the need to expand the role of the FCC in financing and refinancing Canadian farms. With that in mind 1 am happy to see that the amendments before us will increase the limit on capital the agency is able to receive from the government. With a larger capital pool the FCC will be able to borrow more money for its operation.
I mentioned before that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture asked the government earlier this year to increase the capital of the FCC. This bill allows for an increase in the capital limit of some $75 million, but there is no assurance that it will be approved for use by the agency next year. We are still waiting for an announcement from the government about how much additional capital it will provide for the agency in the next year. If the government does not come through quickly with a substantial increase in capital for the FCC, many more of the family farms the minister wishes to preserve as stable and viable entities will go under. While the increase of $75 million will eventually mean an additional almost $2 billion in credit, I fear it will be too little and too late.
I have some reservations too about provisions in the proposed legislation which grant the Farm Credit Corporation the authority to turn to the private market for funds. Let me say that our party is generally not opposed to authority being granted to borrow from sources other than the government. We appreciate that such authority opens more channels from which to borrow funds and that it permits the agency to respond more rapidly to increases in demand for farm credit; but the way in which the authority was announced leaves me with a number of questions. For example, how much of its funding will the Farm Credit Corporation obtain from government and how much from private sources? Will the cost of borrowing from the private market be higher than borrowing from the government, or will provisions be made to encourage investors to provide money to the FCC at less than market rate? Will the authority for the Farm Credit Corporation to turn to the private market for funding in the end really mean higher interest rates for farmers? The intentions of the government in this regard are not clear.
Farm Loans
I can only hope that the minister will heed the plea of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that interest rates of 14 per cent are all that farmers can afford to pay, and ensure the authority granted to the agency to borrow on the private market will mean a reduction from the current 16.75 per cent interest rate.
Last week my colleague, the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, spelled out a number of provisions which would allow the FCC to obtain funds on the private market for some two thirds of the market rate. I hope the minister heard them and will act on my colleague's recommendations.
The amendments in this bill will transfer the statutory loan limits from the act to regulations. 1 appreciate that that will provide opportunities to the agency to increase loan limits more rapidly than at present. I am glad to hear that the minister announced in the House last week his intention to increase the limits on farm credit loans from $200,000 to $300,000 for individual applicants and from $400,000 to $500,000 for groups of two or more applicants, but the minister did not mention whether the transfer from the act to the regulations of the statutory limit for Indian bands will mean a similar increase. I hope Indian bands applying for FCC loans will see an increase in their statutory limit as well.
I hope, too, that with its new authority to amend the statutory loan limits the government will make every effort to ensure they keep pace with the ever-increasing costs of farming.
I am heartened that, in addition to making provision for more rapid increases in statutory loan limits, Bill C-88 will end age discrimination in the agency. I am speaking, of course, about the requirement that applicants for loans to establish farms be under the age of 35. I am sure hon. members of this House understand that starting a farm is a very expensive undertaking and becoming more so every day. Five hundred thousand dollars does not buy a very large prairie farm these days. It is not unusual for new farmers to have to work and save for quite a number of years before they can even consider investing in their own farms. An age limit of 35 does not give many new farmers much time to build up the capital pools they need before investing in farms.
Last April one of my constituents wrote to me about his encounter with age discrimination in this act. He is not an old man at all-he is only 39-but when he applied for a farm credit loan to help him begin farming on a full-time basis the farm he had bought in 1978, he was refused. He was refused not because he was not in need of the money, nor because he was a poor credit risk; he was refused because at the age of 39 he was too old. It is a pretty sad state of affairs when someone is declared too old at the still tender age of 39.
My constituent and I were not alone in our charge that the Farm Credit Act discriminates on the basis of age. In its 1980 annual report to Parliament the Human Rights Commission urged the government to amend the Farm Credit Act to remove this age differential. It said:
The Canadian Human Rights Commission agrees that it is desirable to provide for a phase-in period for farming operations to become established. We

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
recommend, however, that non-discriminatorv criteria be adopted for determining eligibility for a "phase-in farm loan", and in particular that an age limit of 35 no longer be imposed.
I promised my constituent last spring Mr. Speaker, that I would pursue amendments to the Farm Credit Act that would put an end to age discrimination until they were passed by this House.
1 would like to mention in passing that my involvement with this particular case of age discrimination was an education in the machinations of Parliament. Although 1 do not consider myself a rookie, I have to admit I was both confused and a little perturbed about the rules members of this House have to operate under when they want to change legislation. When I first became aware, last spring, that the Farm Credit Act contained this discriminatory clause, I tried to have a private members' bill drafted which would right the wrong.
I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that only ministers of the Crown are allowed to introduce bills which spend taxpayers' money. Most of our ministers are good at this sort of thing, even outside the House of Commons, when they like to jet about in government-owned JetStars or treat journalists to pricey lunches. When I wrote to the law department of the House of Commons to outline and have drafted a private member's bill which would eliminate age discrimination in the Farm Credit Act, I had no idea I was setting myself up for weeks of wrangling and complicated correspondence with the legal department of the House. The result of this wrangling was a ruling from the lawyers that in hoping to introduce a private member's bill I was completely out of order. It seems that the rules of the House say that a bill such as the one I wanted to introduce has the effect of, and I quote, "infringing on the financial initiative of the Crown, not only if it increases the amount but also if it extends the objects and purposes or relaxes the conditions and qualifications" of an act of Parliament.
It did not make much sense to me then and I am not sure it makes much sense to me now how I would be "infringing on the financial initiative of the Crown" by having age discrimination removed from the Farm Credit Act. I was not asking that the government allocate more money to the Farm Credit Corporation. I was only asking that the same government, which at that very time, last spring, was drafting its democratic and glorious Charter of Rights and Freedoms, remove from the books a discriminatory clause in one of its acts. I am happy to see the amendment I sought has finally been introduced.
We in this corner of the House viewed this bill as being somewhat less than we had hoped for. We look forward to dealing with the bill in committee where my colleague, the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, among others, will bring forward a number of suggestions to make it a better piece of legislation.
We are thankful that after five years of delays the bill has finally come before us. We hope that it will only be the first step in a desperately needed major overhaul of agricultural
policy in this country. If our farm community is to survive, it must be done.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: FARM CREDIT ACT FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in this debate to amend the Farm Credit Act. I think it is quite significant that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) should bring forward this piece of very positive legislation at this time. 1 want to congratulate him for laying the groundwork to provide a solid foundation for agriculture. First of all, I should like to refer to the agricultural food strategy report "Challenge for Growth" which was released last fall. That report laid out the policy direction for agriculture in the eighties and I believe has been well received by the farming community, particularly in Ontario. The task force report of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, released in late November, 1981, states that the 1981 Agriculture Canada discussion paper "Challenge for Growth-an AgriFood Policy for Canada," while having certain weaknesses, appears to provide an opportunity to develop short and longterm agricultural policies for the provinces and for Canada as a whole.
I believe that paper has gone a long way toward meeting the objectives and needs of this nation. I believe very strongly that the legislation before us goes on to fill the needs addressed in the recommendations of that task force report, particularly from the federal government standpoint. However, a wide gap remains as far as the other policies are concerned.
The minister has put in place the Meat Import Act which was passed in December. That legislation was requested by the producers of this nation. We have made the Small Business Development Bond available to unincorporated farmers in order to help them through times of low prices, particularly those engaged in red meat production. A week ago today the Canagrex legislation was introduced for second reading. This legislation will expand our agricultural industry and utilize the potential of Canadian producers. It will provide markets for increased productivity as the potential of the industry is developed. The agri-food strategy report indicated that we have the potential for much higher production but unfortunately the market system is not in place to take advantage of it.
I believe the minister was very astute in laying the groundwork to put our industry on a firm foundation before introducing the Farm Credit Corporation legislation. I want to commend him for taking this very firm and sensible approach, rather than injecting new financing into the industry in a hodge-podge fashion. It has always been my experience that you do not borrow yourself out of debt.
I also want to commend the minister for the amendments that will allow the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow on outside markets to supplement its loan fund. It is an investment in the future of this nation. Many farmers and lending institutions would be very happy to invest in this sector, not because of the high returns at the present time but because food is the first essential of human life. The corporation's borrowing authority will be raised from $150 million to $225 million; that is a 50 per cent increase. This is particularly
February 1, 1982

important because the corporation would otherwise have reached its maximum borrowing authority early in 1982-83.
Bill C-88 also removes the age limit in the phasing-in program and allows borrowers over 35 years of age to work off the farm for the first five years. Last summer I learned of an instance where a farm wife made application for additional funds because her husband was over the age limit. It is a credit to the minister that this discriminatory clause was removed from the bill.
The bill proposes to transfer the loan limits from the act to regulations. This will allow the corporation to react more quickly to the demands of the industry and the ever-changing need for credit. In addition, it will be able to disburse up to 30 per cent of a loan on the basis of available security until mortgage registration and other security arrangements for the loan are completed. It will be able to rebate 5 per cent of the interest on loans provided for in the recent budget and it will be able to authorize the corporation to lend a farming corporation money which is to be used as a grant or loan to one of the children who wants to become involved in the family farm corporation.
Certainly the increase in the number of directors will give the corporation a broader base of expertise in a sector which is so important to the total industry.
This is a very positive piece of legislation. Perhaps in one sense it should have come forward sooner, but I remind hon. members of the opposition that the minister amended this piece of legislation four times during his tenure, every 2.5 years, which is in keeping with the changes that have taken place in the agri-food sector over the past ten years. There have been some very dramatic changes in Canadian agriculture, in terms not only of the number of farms and farmers, but also the size of and investment in those farms. Indeed it is a credit to the minister that he reacted quickly to the changing needs of the industry.
We must bear in mind that the corporation was originally intended only as a lender of last resort. In this context we changed the legislation as needed. It is interesting that credit unions provide approximately 20 per cent of the line of credit to farmers, banks about 23 per cent, and the Farm Credit Corporation about 25 per cent. We are looking at the main source of financing and funding of the agricultural industry in Canada. It has been a good investment for Canadians, especially when we consider that 90 per cent of all loans were made to family farms. At the moment about 93 per cent of all Farm Credit Corporation loans are in good standing. The majority of these loans were made to individuals who could not obtain funding elsewhere. This is a credit not only to the FCC but to the industry as a whole. Since 1959 the FCC has assisted over
160,000	Canadian farmers, 114,000 of whom still have loans with the corporation.
The amendments before us today and the other economic legislation passed in December are the basis upon which we must build if we are to meet the potential outlined in the
Farm Loans
agri-food strategy last fall. When the amendments about which we are speaking today are passed and the Canagrex legislation is finalized, I trust Canadian farmers and their organizations will move quickly to avail themselves of all available legislation, to expand production and to seek out and develop long-term markets. All these steps were taken at the request of Canadian farmers. This is the way it should happen in a democratic society. The government has reacted in all these areas.
Now that we have these bills before us, it is up to the farmers, their organizations and the provincial governments to move forward. These bills indicate the commitment and concern of the federal government for the need of a healthy agri-food industry. The main financial bill, as far as farmers are concerned, has been amended on four occasions under the term of the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). A huge influx of capital into the industry above that laid out in the legislation would be irresponsible. We all know what happens in such an event-land prices increase very rapidly in value, prices spiral, and it ends up that young farmers are not helped. A huge influx of capital could set off another spiral of inflationary factors and make it completely unrealistic for farmers to expect a monetary return from their farms which would provide them with livelihoods. The situation would be worse than that of today's. The minister has been responsible in the manner in which he has drafted the legislation. We can go forward and make adjustments by regulation, as need arises, and not trigger another round of inflationary prices in the land sector.
The passing of the other legislation to which I referred earlier, the broadening of the base to allow the corporation to borrow outside the government, the raising of the corporation's borrowing authority by 50 per cent, the removing of the age limit, the providing of a disbursement of up to 30 per cent of a loan on the basis of available securities, the allowing of the corporation to respond more quickly to changing conditions, and certainly the allowing of persons to borrow in order to purchase shares of family farm corporations, are all very positive amendments which reflect our changing industry. Last but not least, the broadening of the base of expertise among members of the corporation will result in a better understanding of the needs of farmers across the nation.
In view of the very positive legislation before us today, 1 hope and trust that Canadian farmers will not only look at this legislation but at the agri-food strategy report which pointed out the opportunities ahead of us. They should look at the Meat Import Act which was passed last December. They should look at the Canagrex legislation which will assist them to take advantage of ever-increasing markets in this hungry world. We should bear in mind that Canada is one of four countries which are net exporters of food. We should focus on agriculture as Canadians working in partnership, farmers working with each other, processors and packers working together, not as Canadians from eastern Canada competing against Canadians from western Canada for the same market.

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
We should allow our food to be exported in an orderly manner, to bring into focus the potential which exists in Canada.
I call on the provinces to come to agreement as quickly as possible and to bring about a harmonization of the stabilization programs across the nation, rather than each province following a system of their own, or each province competing against others in a manner which puts one province at a very distinct disadvantage to that of another, 1 firmly believe that we must correct this situation if we are to achieve the great potential which exists in Canada. Agricultural organizations and provincial governments should examine their roles in this very essential industry.
Earlier I referred to the task force report of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. It realized there has to be assistance from provincial governments to producers. It was strongly suggested that the government of Ontario bring forward a loan program to assist its young farmers get established.
It is no accident that that report reflects many of the things that we have brought forward as legislation before this House this last couple of months. Certainly these three major bills have been in the works for many months. But it is the understanding the federal minister had of this industry that what was brought forward was done so in a very responsible manner, a manner that laid the firm foundation to which I referred earlier. The foundations are laid. But the total industry-and I include the farmers, the processors and the packers-the provincial governments and certainly this House all have to examine their roles in these times of changing forces in the marketplace.
When one considers the concentration of power at the retail level and the fact that only a few supermarket chains control about 70 per cent of our retail food sales, if the farmer is to survive then we have to have a countervailing force in the marketplace. The legislation is there, and I trust the farmers of Canada will use it to their advantage.
Certainly the legislation before us today goes a long way toward meeting the requirements of Canadian farmers for the foreseeable future. But no doubt in another couple of years the legislation will have to be amended and updated.
There are other areas to which I think we must respond, but I do not think the time is ripe for it yet. When you set up a financial package, that package has to be prepared, as I indicated earlier, in a very responsible manner, a manner that will not trigger another round of spiralling land values, values that with today's commodity prices could not give a proper return on investment.
It is in this context that I urge hon. members of this House to pass this bill as quickly as possible to relieve the financial problems before us in the agricultural sector of Canada.

speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie)-Veterans Affairs-Entitlement to retroactive pension payments; the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble)- Finance-Effect of budget on employees meeting increased accommodation costs following transfers, (b) Request that provision affecting mortgages be postponed; the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle)-External Affairs-El Salvador-Holding of democratic elections, (b) Recognition of political movement.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Whelan that Bill C-88, respecting loans to farmers, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak today on Bill C-88. Before I confine my remarks to Bill C-88, I would like to comment on the remarks made by the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson). He pointed out very clearly in his address to the House that the legislation fills the needs, particularly where the federal government is concerned, he said. I would agree that most of the legislation passed in this House meets the needs, particularly where the federal government is concerned. Very little thought, very little attention is given to the people who are being legislated, and I might add legislated to death.
The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex also said that the Small Business Development Bond was made available in the last budget to unincorporated farmers. The hon. member forgot to say unincorporated farmers in dire straits. In other words, the Small Business Development Bond was made available but only to farmers in dire straits. I have yet in my riding to find one farmer who has been approved for a Small Business Development Bond since the budget was introduced last year, even a farmer in dire straits. The terminology itself does not define for the banks or the lending institutions what is dire straits. I agree with the hon. member that investment in the farm community right across this country is indeed an invest-
February 1, 1982

ment in the future of this country. When you get right down to it, you cannot eat refrigerators, or cars, or drink oil.
The producers are men in the farm community who create wealth in our land. It has been estimated that 48 per cent of all the wealth in Canada is created by the farming community.
The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex complimented the minister for the removal of the age limit for farm credit loans. But it was the same government that implemented the act, enacted the legislation which put that provision in in the first place. His comment escapes me. It seems to me that if you put something into legislation and then a few days later remove the provision and say you have done a marvellous thing, you must not forget who it was who put it in the legislation in the first place. Other members of this House have indicated some of the problems that has created. Nevertheless, I am glad that provision was removed.
My hon. friend from Lambton-Middlesex also said that this legislation was put in place at the request of farmers, as it should be in a democratic society.
How about interest rates? Are the farmers supporting the unconscionably high interest rates that are affecting the whole Canadian economy? Are not the people of Canada saying that interest rates are too high? Are Canadians not asking the government to do something about high interest rates? Maybe that kind of input is not accepted in this democratic chamber, as the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex suggests.
How about the fight which the cattlemen are having now with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan)? Cattlemen are resisting with all their efforts the controls which they see the Minister of Agriculture trying to impose on them. They are fiercely independent cattle producers and they are saying: "No, government, stay out of our business; we will handle it."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order with respect to the remark about controls. I think the hon. member should not be suggesting that the minister will impose controls.

If the heat is getting too much for the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, he should get out of the kitchen.
The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex mentioned that this legislation was introduced at the request of the farmers, as it should in a democratic society. Those are his words as close as I can recall. I am only pointing that out to him. What about the cattlemen? They are expressing the same thing with regard to the farm community. Do these people not belong to the farm community? They are giving input to the minister. What is the minister doing? He is attempting with everything at his disposal to beat them down. It is a disgraceful situation. But, of course, that is another kind of democracy. Maybe it is only
Farm Loans
democracy and he should return to the words of the hon. member who said that the legislation fills the needs, particularly where the federal government is concerned. I underline that because that is exactly what the hon. member said.
The hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) said they were putting an extremely high priority on this bill. It was mentioned two years ago-that is high priority. Last spring the minister was running around saying, "We have to do something about the Farm Credit Corporation. I am going to introduce legislation." It was promised for last fall. Well, we are now into February. Certainly we support this kind of legislation, but if it had been in place when it should have been, we would have something like 250 to 300 farmers still producing. Instead, they have gone bankrupt, or were foreclosed and are no longer producing.
The hon. member said input costs are up and he gave some excellent statistics. Gasoline is up 70 per cent, diesel fuel 80 per cent or more-I am not sure of the figures. The prices of pesticide, fertilizer, machinery and parts are up. Interest rates are up. Then he said that returns are down. That same member then alluded to the Small Business Development Bond, this great saviour mentioned in the budget. I have yet to find one unincorporated farmer in dire straits, healthy straits or any kind of straits, who has received approval under that bond. I challenge other members to bring them forward to see how many we have. They know full well this was a political gimmick. It has been a useful tool, that is all. Perhaps their ghost writers are the same, Mr. Speaker, I do not know, but they both said they support this bill and they want all members to support it and the other legislation that is coming. We have been hearing that for the last two years.
We basically support the bill giving the FCC authority to seek supplementary funds in the private money market. However, we do not support it unless there is a firm commitment by the government that support to the FCC will not be decreased.
Canada's agricultural industry is sincerely hurting. I have had people from every line of business in the agricultural sector phoning me day after day. They can see their life's work going down the tube after 30 or 40 years because, as the hon. member for Algoma said, their costs are up. They say the return is not there, they cannot make it go. Where is the help over the rough edges for those farmers?
This government will guarantee millions upon millions of dollars in loans to prop up the automobile and manufacturing industries, and yet it sits idly by when it comes to a very basic industry such as agriculture. It points to these red herrings: "Look at the Small Business Development Bond." Well, they cannot get it. We are going to allow the FCC to go out and get money elsewhere in the market. They say, "Boy, isn't that a good thing?" Well, it is in one respect.
The budget itself, what did it do? The Minister of Agriculture went around the country saying, "Wait until this legislation comes through, wait until the budget comes through; you

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
will see how much this is going to help. I have the answers for the farmers; wait and see." Well, we waited, and what happened, Mr. Speaker? The government changed the capital gains tax reserve to the detriment of the farmer. It eliminated completely the income-averaging annuity contracts. For expansion purposes it eliminated the Small Business Development Bond to the unincorporated farmer. The budget gave the Farm Credit Corporation $50 million and said, "Spread it around, you have more money to lend." It is estimated by every authoritative source in Canada that they needed at least $450 to $500 million more.
I suggest to you and to all members of the House, Mr. Speaker, that Bill C-88, while it is needed, will not provide the necessary short-term relief to enable the farming community to stay in business.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, we will support this legislation, but will the government give a firm commitment that its direct funding to the FCC will continue and not be cut back by way of sleight of hand as were transfer payments to the provinces? Why was this bill introduced three years too late? That is the question. Had it been there when it should have been, those farmers forced into bankruptcy might still be producing, and this government must accept the blame for this idiocy. In addition to those who went into bankruptcy, Mr. Speaker, hundreds were forced out of business through foreclosure and forced sale. This occurred because these are proud people and they said, "No way; I am getting out, getting my money out and getting out of here." These are men who put their hands to the soil years ago; generations of men who came here, Mr. Speaker, and said they were going to break the soil, develop it, grow food and create wealth in this country.
Where is the assistance to get those interest rates down which are affecting the farm community and, indeed, every other community? Where is the assistance which will bring the price of fertilizer to a reasonable level so that the input costs of farmers will not be astronomical? Where is the assistance for fuel oil, diesel fuel and gasoline so that a farmer can go out and plant his crop without being hit by unconscionably higher prices for his fuel? Where is the action toward moving the commodities to market? Where is all this action, this doubletracking? Where will we go with the commodity to feed the world? How will we get it to the world to feed the world? When will the government be prepared to admit to the House that interest rates are not holding down inflation but are adding to it because they are adding to the input costs of the farm community right across Canada? Someone must pay the interest cost.
Farmers are a fiercely independent lot. They do not ask for much. They only ask what any normal working man requests; that is, a little bit of reward for their efforts. Why should a farmer not expect a small return on his investment, not only his investment in money but also in time and effort? Is he not entitled to this? He certainly is entitled.
What would happen tomorrow if there were no farmers available in Canada to produce the food that we eat? We have long victimized farmers and the agricultural community. They have long been victimized. It is time that we looked at that problem seriously. We are prepared to subsidize prospective laywers so that they can go through university. Has Your Honour ever figured out the cost? I wonder if anyone has ever sat down to figure out the cost of putting one lawyer, one doctor, one dentist or one engineer through school. Then a government like this comes along and puts in a national energy policy and a budget so that the only ones who will benefit, of course, will be the lawyers and the accountants who stay behind, but the rest of the professions move out, saying, "Let us move to the States or find another place to live."
I think it is time that we seriously looked at the agricultural community and did right by it. The hon. member for Algoma mentioned increasing the number on the board of the Farm Credit Corporation from five to seven members. He stated that the workload of the Farm Credit Corporation is becoming so tremendous, so monumental, that they must get two more men. The board of directors of the Farm Credit Corporation does not do the day to day business; surely, the hon. member for Algoma knows that. The board sets policy; surely, the hon. member for Algoma knows that. I say to hon. members that five men can set as much policy as seven men, and can set it clearly and concisely. I would suggest, in all humility, that the expansion of the board from five to seven members is just another opportunity for the present Liberal government to do a little more pork-barrelling.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are listening to you.

I am glad the hon. member is listening to me. I hope he is learning something.
1 can remember times when farmers were told to plant barley from fencerow to fencerow,-
Concession road to concession road.

-when the markets were lacking, there were no markets, and we all know what happened. We see headline after headline: "Farm bankruptcies up 28 per cent." Nothing can help such a situation. The Farm Credit Corporation will not help that. The help must be directed at the commodity price. We must somehow get the farmers over these short-term dire straits they are in. What is the forecast for 1982? A drop in farm incomes is seen. In every paper that one wants to pick up one reads that every economist across the country is forecasting a drop in farm income for 1982. We are still not addressing that, to our shame.
Another headline states, "1982 Forecast to be Even Tougher Year for Farmers Caught in a Cost-Price Squeeze." This comes from the economist for the federal Department of Agriculture, George Andrusiak. He states:
Farm returns are expected to drop or, at best, remain stable for most agricultural products, while virtually every farm cost is expected to rise. The result is that the cost-price squeeze will tighten its grip on farmers right across the country.
How does this affect the manufacturing sector? Indeed, how does it affect every sector? Farm machinery sales have been hit by revised tax regulation. It goes right to the budget. The farmer does not have his capital cost allowance to write off and he will not buy.
Farm Loans
What did the Minister of Agriculture do? He spent a good part of last fall running around the country, blaming the banks for the high interest rates. Even a neophyte minister with no understanding whatsoever of an economic situation knows full well that it is not the banks that control interest rates but government policy. The policy of this government is to keep interest rates high.
Few sectors of the economy are as dependent on borrowed money as is agriculture. Farmers need money to start their operations and to remain in business. Most of their costs are Fixed. They cannot cut labour costs because labour is not that kind of factor. They cannot cut their feed bill because the animals would starve. If they do not fertilize this year, they will not get as high a yield next year. That is something the members of this House do not understand.
The national farm debt for just over 300,000 farmers has reached $16.6 billion. With 10 per cent interest rates, most producers can manage, but they cannot manage at 18 or 20 per cent. Because they do not control the price of the commodity they produce, they cannot pass on their increased interest rate costs to the consumer. That is what makes the farmer hurt.
When the farmer hurts, the commerce of the country hurts. Commercial enterprise everywhere gets into trouble. One need only look at what happened to Massey-Ferguson, as well as the implement dealers in farm communities across this country. If we look at the farmers in the farm community, we see what is happening.
The government should adopt a program which would place a moratorium on farm debt, stop foreclosures and forced sales. This government has it in its power to raise interest rates in excess of 20 per cent in order to protect the dollar and, so they say, fight inflation. They must therefore have it in their power to place a moratorium on farm debt.
It is this government which provides millions of dollars for foreign aid and programs which at best are questionable. It provides loans to such countries as Mexico and supports sales to certain foreign countries at very low interest rates, yet it leaves the most basic and fundamental resource in this country, namely agriculture, with a high interest rate policy.
There should be an immediate infusion of $500 million into the Farm Credit Corporation in order to subsidize interest rates and increase the loan programs for farmers. This must be done because if we do not do this, the day will come when there will be shortages in the supermarkets in the large urban centres in some very fundamental areas.
Just once the government should adopt the suggestion of a couple of members opposite. The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex talked about democracy. Let us bring in the farmers who till the soil, get their hands dirty doing it, and plant the crops that we need, to help us draft a policy. We should get away from this ivory tower in which we sit. Let the farm representatives monitor the Small Business Development Bond. The government should come forward with a bit of truth

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
and honesty and say what the Small Business Development Bond is doing, "It is not doing the job we thought it would, so let's change it". For once the government should say it made a mistake and is prepared to make the necessary changes.
What is wrong with allowing farmers to use the Small Business Development Bond to build up their operations? If some farmers could get a loan against their equity, they could make their operation much more productive, they could streamline it. Instead, we have the government saying that the Small Business Development Bond is only for those unincorporated farmers who are in dire straits.
We should create a market insurance plan for farmers, one to which both the federal and provincial governments can contribute as well as the farmers. This would protect the income of farmers who do not have access to the unemployment insurance offices. We must be more enlightened and find a way of doing this. I am sure we can. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
