speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. When the House rose at six o'clock, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to sum up by saying that we on this side of the House support this legislation provided that the government does not intend to cut back on its financial commitment to the Farm Credit Corporation. Other than for reasons of patronage, I fail to see why the government proposes to expand the board of the Farm Credit Corporation from five to seven members. To me, it is purely and simply pork-barrelling.
We on this side believe that the Farm Credit Corporation should be provided with an additional $500 million because this legislation will not solve the difficulties which farmers are experiencing today or provide the short-term funding which they need. The extra $50 million provided for in the budget is not sufficient. There is still no help for the farmers on a short-term basis. This is an oversight by the government which must be addressed. The legislation before us is too little too late.

Mr. Speaker, in connection with the tabling of Bill C-88, I should like to give a brief history of the Farm Credit Corporation, outlining the progress made since it was founded, especially since the corporation is 22 years old today. In this brief overview we shall see how the corporation has progressed, how many millions of dollars have
been invested in Canada's agriculture and finally, I shall say a few words about how our agricultural sector has evolved and stress the energy and initiative shown by our Canadian farmers. When I say that Canadian farmers have shown energy and initiative during the past few years, Mr. Speaker, I should add that, although it is often said that millions of dollars are poured into Canada's agriculture, I feel that if every dollar spent in Canadian industry had been as productive as the same dollar spent on agriculture, we might not be experiencing as great a recession as we are now. Let me give an example. Only 20 years ago, one farmer was able to feed not more than ten people, while today he is able to feed at least 40. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it must be recognized that investment in the agricultural sector has been very productive. Now, if I may, I shall start my brief history.
The Farm Credit Corporation was founded in 1959 with a capital of $8 million. The purpose was to provide funds for a first mortgage, to purchase a farm, fertilizer, seed, livestock, equipment and buildings and also to improve land and pay off debts. The loan ceiling at the time was $20,000 or 75 per cent of the value of the farm, while loans of up to $26,000 were granted to farmers under 45 with at least five years' experience in farming. A second type of loan consisted in a 40 per cent loan guarantee on livestock and implements. In 1961, the corporation's capital was increased to $12 million.
Regulations were amended to allow for the increase in value of grazing land when part of the land was leased from the Crown. In 1962, capital was increased to $16 million. In 1964, the loan ceiling rose from $20,000 to $40,000 per unit. Loans were authorized to farmers wishing to help a family member get started in farming. More people became eligible for loans which were authorized for a wider variety of reasons. In 1968, capital was increased to $40 million. Loans could go as high as $80,000 when the farm had two owner-operators, and up to $100,000 with three owner-operators. In that same year, it became possible to obtain loans representing 90 per cent of the value of land and livestock, provided one of the owner-operators was under 35 and had proved to be an outstanding administrator. In 1972, capital was increased to $6 million and the loan ceiling raised to $100,000 for first and second category farmers. The minimum age of 21 was abolished. Only Canadian citizens and landed immigrants were eligible for loans. In 1975, the corporation's capital was raised to $100 million. Farmers under 35 became eligible for loans of up to $150,000. The FCC also authorized loans representing 100 per cent of the market value of land, livestock and implements. In 1978, capital was increased to $150 million. The FCC authorized loans of up to $200,000 for a farm enterprise headed by a qualified operator and up to $400,000 for a farm with more than one qualified operator.
Mr. Speaker, when Bill C-88 is passed, the FCC will have a capital of $125 million. It is clear there has been a substantial
February 1, 1982

improvement in procedures and increase in capital of the Farm Credit Corporation. In 1981, 75,000 FCC borrowers were active in the agricultural sector throughout Canada. This was a brief outline of the Farm Credit Corporation, which is 22 years old this year. Of course I had to omit a number of important facts which would have taken too long to enumerate. In any case, from this brief history it is clear that the FCC has continued to progress and to adapt to the growing needs of modern agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on enumerating a number of interesting and useful statistics, but I prefer to discuss the importance of investment in agriculture today and the reasons why the FCC evolved as it has. I would like to stress the importance of our modern farming operations. People say that millions of dollars are spent on agriculture and they wonder why. Let me take a dairy farm as an example. Dairy herds are extremely valuable, and because of the rigours of our winters, farm buildings must meet very high standards, especially barns for dairy herds which are very sensitive to cold temperatures, all of which requires a considerable investment. Farmland has increased tremendously in value, so that prospective farmers are faced with very substantial expenditures if they are to purchase farmland and farm machinery.
A few years ago, a 100 horsepower tractor could be bought for $10,000. Ten years later, the same tractor is worth $35,000. The House will agree that all these investments constitute a considerable burden on the farmer, and it is only fair that we should help farmers by granting them broader credit facilities. Another example is our grain producers in western Canada, with thousands of acres of very valuable, very fertile and very high-yield land. Grain producers need huge silos and storage room to keep seed, fertilizers and farm marchinery, all of which runs into thousands if not millions of dollars per farm unit. I should also like to say a few words about the market gardening sector, which is certainly not negligible and requires far more specialized equipment for its highly specialized operations.
We could talk about commercial production and about large scale potato production in Ontario, in Quebec, in Prince Edward Island, in New Brunswick and elsewhere. We could talk about pieces of land. With respect to commercial producers, especially in southern Ontario where farms are of outstanding quality and very expensive to buy, we could mention the fact that those people must have very well equipped and very modern refrigerated warehouses. We could mention the seeds as well as the huge quantities of fertilizers and pesticides which those producers must use. We could also mention the machinery and the marketing costs to point out once again the need for financing which is even better geared to the requirements of our ever-expanding contemporary agriculture which also has to cope with the rising costs of new machinery, lands and all the inputs required for that production.
Farm Loans
We often meet people who still believe that agriculture has not evolved, and that is why we must learn more about the evolution of Canada's agriculture. And of course we must also talk about the risks involved. We know that the farmer has a plant without a roof and he has to protect himself against a great many natural elements. In a plant with a roof it is possible to program the production or the sales, to predict months in advance which way things will go. But on a farm the producer is up against natural elements such as drought, ground humidity and climatic conditions which often are not conducive to plant growth, a whole series of factors which will result in lower yield. There are not just risks in farming, however, there is indeed a very positive side to it. When there are risks, the farmer does have means to protect himself, such as stabilization payments and crop insurance which are funded by the various levels of government, federal and provincial, and the producer as well. We also have marketing boards, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to refer briefly to the establishment of some of them.
Recently, many Canadian organizations have criticized our marketing boards. I admit they might not be the ideal or perfect instrument, but I invite anyone who has a better answer to tell us about it while there is still time, so that our farmers can continue to make a living in agriculture and consumers can continue to pay reasonable prices, because if the farmer cannot have a decent return, the consumer will necessarily have to pay for it. In this regard, I disagree completely with the suggestion of the Economic Council of Canada that we should abolish the marketing boards, in this way Canadian farmers could no longer control their production. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I believe that if anyone is aware of the situation and knows what he wants, it is certainly the Canadian farm producer. As I said at the outset it would be a good thing if the Canadian industry as a whole could be as effective as our Canadian farmers, because if one sector of our economy has remained healthy and prosperous, it is certainly agriculture.
Some sectors obviously have problems. Western beef producers have problems. Eastern pork producers are having difficulties, but these are obviously cyclical productions. Hon. members on both sides of the House who want the Canadian farmer to be successful will find an answer, and I hope that they can do so as soon as possible to avoid a disaster. I said earlier that as recently as 20 years ago, one farm producer could feed ten people and that he now feeds 40. I believe that those who read such statements and who are aware of the dynamic attitude of the Canadian farmer can only urge the Canadian government to make more funds available to the Canadian agricultural industry since we have positive proof of the evolution and dynamic nature of our farm industry. 1 would like to give an example of what I mean. We have to support our farmers and provide them with necessary mechanisms even

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
though it has often been said in the past that farmers are always subsidized, but that is where all discussions and arguments stop.
As a member who is somewhat aware of the problems of our farm producers, I have argued with people on both sides of the House, that the Canadian government should continue to pay $2.66 a hundredweight for milk exports. There are two schools of thought in this regard. Some people simply want this subsidy to be abolished because they feel the farmer is oversubsidized. However, if this subsidy of $2.66 were abolished tomorrow morning, dairy products, mainly butter, and also cheese, could increase by about 40 cents a pound. This may be called a direct subsidy to the farmer, but I wonder if it is not the consumer who benefits most from it is not the main beneficiary. I could give many similar examples, but 1 believe that this one is enough and that those who read my statements or hear me now will realize that the farmer needs to be supported and that this is always to the advantage of the consumer.
In the past, every time I have sat on a committee on agriculture and elsewhere, l have always invited those who design or write legislation to treat farmers more and more as businessmen. I have even thought of suggesting regulations which would give farmers an incentive to make advance payments to replenish the Farm Credit Corporation funds, which are often depleted on account of a large number of requests. I reiterate now that proposal because 1 think it would be an excellent way to have instalments paid ahead of time and the funds of the Farm Credit Corporation replenished.
Last year, I stated in a committee that if a farmer were allowed to make advance payments of $1,000, $2,000, $3,000 and up to $5,000 annually, such instalments would not be considered as income and would be tax free. 1 can assure you that the more productive farmers would be encouraged to anticipate their payments and that would inspire others to do likewise. The tax-exempt status of such payments would be similar to that of subsidies enjoyed by owners of businesses in the private sector. Once more, I hope the suggestion will be considered and that others will help support the reasoning behind it. I would also be in favour of including an interest rate review as part of the reorganization of the FCC, so that when a farmer contracts a loan, it is not "closed" for the entire duration of the loan, which may be 25 years. A few months ago I wrote to the Minister of Agriculture to suggest this amendment. Nowadays it would be quite feasible. We have
74,000	loans outstanding across Canada. It would be easy to have a kind of automatic computerized update whenever interest rates drop by an average of 2 per cent, at which time all farm credit loans would be adjusted instead of waiting 15 or 20 years, whenever the loans are due.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should all congratulate the present minister, who has constantly been amending the Farm Credit Act, and we should also congratulate him on the birth last
week of the new Canagrex corporation, which is to be the umbrella organization for a host of agricultural agencies that can be expected to stimulate Canadian farm production. In the past we have had some serious problems with marketing. That is understandable, because we have many commodities that are now being produced under the quota system. However, with Canagrex, I believe people will begin to understand that we must be aggressive in our approach to export markets, especially since our Canadian products have an excellent reputation worldwide. Once more, 1 am convinced that with the energy and initiative they are capable of mustering and with all the tools and structures that have been put into place in recent years, Canadian farmers will be satisfactorily equipped to cope with difficult times such as we are now experiencing. As I already pointed out, the fact that equipment, land and in fact any input that is part of agriculture today is tremendously expensive, the availability of additional funds will encourage young people to enter the farming business in this country, and if our farmers remain productive and dynamic, I am sure that all Canadian consumers will benefit. 1 sincerely hope that Bill C-88 is passed, for the good of all Canadian farmers.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure at this time to address a few remarks to the House on Bill C-88 which is designed to help the agricultural community. Half of the riding of Simcoe North is engaged in the agricultural economy, thus this bill is very important to the people who live there and deal mainly in beef cattle, dairy cattle and cash crops. I should like to address a few remarks to the specifics of the bill-the purpose of allowing the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow supplementary funding, the interest rate rebate provisions of the budget, the increase in the membership of the board of directors, and the removal of the 35-year age limit. But before doing so, I want to deal with some of the problems which we know interface with the provisions of the increase in farm credit funding.
In the budget of November 12, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) promised additional funding to farmers in the amount of $45 million for loans. The House will know that is a drop in the bucket compared with what is needed by the agricultural community in Canada. The Liberal Party, and in particular the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), has made a litany of promises throughout 1980 and 1981 as to what the budget would do for farmers. As farm bankruptcies rose 109 per cent from 1979 to 1981, we on this side of the House called for reasonable assistance to Canadian farmers. This bill goes partly toward providing that assistance, but since the situation has worsened, there has been a need to provide additional long-term funding.
What has happened? We provided $45 million when the Canadian Federation of Agriculture calculated that $1 billion was necessary to do the job for Canadian farmers. The Liberal
February 1, 1982

government provided $50 million, of which approximately $11 million was allocated to Ontario. The Ontario Federation of Agriculture calculated that $11 million would not suffice for even one county in Ontario. Representatives of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture appeared before the Progressive Conservative committee meeting in Toronto. They presented a very well-reasoned brief in which they talked about the needs of the farming community. Its president, Ralph Barrie, a farmer himself, was present in person. There was an excellent exchange of viewpoints. Fie suggested to us, and provided us with the facts, that the agricultural community is hurting and that the lack of concern of the Liberal Party is criminal.
Funding for farm credit has declined over the past five years. In 1975 the Farm Credit Corporation lent $641 million; in 1980 it lent $509 million. The $45 million suggested in the budget translates into 450 loans of $100,000 each. This is a pittance when compared with the capital requirements of a Canadian farmer today. It pales even further when one considers that during the first ten months of 1980, 230 farmers across Canada went bankrupt. Over 50 per cent of those bankruptcies were in Ontario. While I welcome the fact that there is more funding, I point out to the House that it is a pittance. The hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) indicated that in the 1980-81 year the Farm Credit Corporation had only provided for 17 per cent of the applications which came to it.
In the November budget presented by the Minister of Finance there was a provision of $5 million to be used to reduce interest rates for farmers. This is an insult to Canadian farmers. They are bearing the brunt of the Liberal high interest rate policy. Farm bankruptcies, power of sale proceedings and foreclosures are all a result of the Liberal high interest rate policy. The government will provide $5 million to reduce interest rates for farmers. At the same time it is considering a loan of $198.5 million through the Canada Development Corporation to allow a Canadian company to bid on a pipeline contract in the Soviet Union. In fact, three interested companies are from Montreal. This is a very sad commentary on the priorities of the Liberal Party. It is more concerned about more money going to the Soviet Union by way of loan or to an engineering firm in Montreal than it is about Canadian farmers one end of the country to the other.
I read about the increase from five to seven on the board of directors. For an extra $50 billion it is hard to understand why the board must be increased by 40 per cent. I am sure the House can imagine the desperate search which is being conducted throughout the country to get people to admit they are Liberals so that they can sit on the board of directors. It must be difficult times for one to admit being a Liberal in order to be part of the board of directors of the Farm Credit Corporation. Jim Coutts is a name which comes to mind. He is a very eminent chap who took a run at Spadina. Perhaps he will take a run at Broadview-Greenwood. Perhaps he will take a look at some other ridings. Mr. Coutts has a very distinguished electoral career. Perhaps he would be quick to get on the board of directors of the Farm Credit Corporation. One might think he
Farm Loans
may even be able to clear his conflict of interests faster than Senator Austin in order to approach that eminent position.
Speaking about the administration of the Farm Credit Corporation, I should like to point out that from my standpoint in Simcoe county, as I indicated to the minister, I find it to be very practical. If the minister could get some of the practical approach of the Farm Credit Corporation people in Simcoe County to be translated to the Federal Business Development Bank, business people would be on his side. The Farm Credit Corporation deals with applications, either approves them or turns them down, whereas the Federal Business Development Bank dances business people around with requests for more and more information, and eventually turns them down. Basically, we in my county are happy with the people who review the loans and make the decisions.
We on this side of the House applaud the removal of the 35-year age limit. Unfortunately it was left in and the government did not remove it before now. At least now it will be possible for every applicant to stand on his or her own merits regardless of age when applying for funds to establish a farming operation. We welcome this step because we do not think anyone should be denied an opportunity to enter the farming community because of age.
While dealing with the financial provisions of the bill, I would like to comment upon the Small Business Development Bond. Much has been made in the House about the extension of the provisions of the Small Business Development Bond to the agricultural community. As it was originally conceived, the extension of the bond to that community would have been a boon, just as it would have been a boon to the business community. But the same provision was put on the bond for farmers as it was for business operations. Now we have a criterion that one must be in desperate or dire straits, or in financial difficulty, before the government comes to the aid of this very important segment of our economy. We can do without widgets, but we cannot do without farm produce or the food which can be grown in our soil. It is about time the government put a priority on the farming community. If it wanted to do something, it could take away financial difficulty. It could expand the financing available for the Farm Credit Corporation. Canadian agriculture deserves a higher priority from the Liberal government than it is getting at the present time.
We welcome the bill. However, we do not think the bill has gone far enough because Canadians are suffering from the impact of high interest rates. The budget did very little for them and, for that matter, for anybody else, but we are pleased to see at least one thing come forward from this government to help the farming community.

Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to be able to say a few words with respect to Bill C-88, an act respecting loans to farmers. 1 commend the minister for finally bringing in this bill. As hon. members are aware, the bill will provide additional funds. It has been

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
mentioned by several speakers on our side that this bill will increase the complement on the board of directors from five to seven. However, some of us wonder whether the minister has a couple of defeated Liberal candidates in mind for these lucrative positions in which they will not be overworked.
He will take one himself.
People appointed to the Farm Credit Corporation are not appointed because of political affiliation.

I am pleased to hear the minister say that the people will not be appointed because of political affiliation. 1 have heard it said before that people are not appointed to boards because of political affiliation but because of ability. However, the strange thing is that appointees are always Liberals and not of any other political persuasion.
Oh, oh!
If you check, you will find that to be incorrect.

In any event, we will wait to see what happens when these appointments are made.
The budget approved is $55 million. While that is a substantial amount of money, it is a far cry from what is really needed. We hope the minister will be able to do a job and sell the cabinet the need for additional sums. It will not take long to use up $55 million.
Everyone agrees that the Farm Credit Corporation has been of great assistance to agriculture and to the industry in Canada over the number of years since its institution, which I believe was in 1959, some 22 years ago. However, this bill has been delayed too long, but it is better late than never. I see the minister paying some attention. Better never late; I think he would agree with that statement.
My colleague, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) was minister of agriculture in the Clark administration during 1979. During that brief period, $50 million was provided for additional farm credit lending. The hon. member for Elgin was planning to provide an additional $100 million in 1980, an additional $150 million in 1981, with $200 million to be added in 1982. This was necessary, in his view, just to keep up with inflation and the rising land costs in the country.
I think we are all in agreement that these costs will not decrease but will actually increase. Farmers require credit. It is important that Canadian people understand that about 15 per cent of the costs paid out by the agricultural industry is for interest. Credit is the number one problem facing farmers in Canada today, and the cost of borrowing money is still very high. Let us hope that the minister will see to it that there is no increase in rates but rather a decrease. The rate of 16.75 per cent is quite a bit for a farmer to carry. The minister, although he is not a farmer now, has been a farmer and is, I am sure, sympathetic.
The provision is in there for a reduced rate of five points, I believe, which gives an interest rate of 11.75 per cent for those farmers who are in dire straits. I have had farmers come to me
stating that they have applied to the Farm Credit Corporation but have been told they are not on the verge of bankruptcy and, therefore, are not eligible for the 11.75 per cent rate. Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) come to the session tonight on this bill, the Farm Credit Act. I think it has been intimated by hon. members who have previously spoken that this is one bit of agricultural legislation which has stood the test of time more than any other. It has not needed serious amendment. At the same time, during the 20-odd years since 1959 that this legislation has been in existence, we have seen a growth rate of productivity in the agricultural sector of about 7 per cent a year compared to a growth rate of about 2 per cent to 3 per cent in the rest of Canada's industrial segments. There is no question but that this first attempt to get a modern farm credit system in Canada has been a success. My remarks tonight will deal almost exclusively with the philosophy of the legislation. I would like to test that philosophy against the amendment we have before us.
The philosophy of the farm credit corporation act of 1959 can be shown by contrasting it against the old farm loans board which was set up in 1934 under the farm loans act of that year. The principles used in the original legislation in 1934 were for the purpose of meeting an existing condition. Many farmers were bankrupt, no one would buy their land and they had no way of paying their debts. Therefore, the government of that time set up the farmers and creditors rearrangement act whereby all a farmer's creditors would come in and calculate how much of a debt would be repaid under the new level of prices, which was very low. All creditors dropped the amounts of their claims and each was repaid a certain proportion of their loan. That act had to be followed by a farm loan act which lent money to the farmers to help repay some of the creditors who were fairly highly secured, getting them off the farmers' backs. The farmers borrowed money from the farm loans board to repay some of these creditors.
That legislation pioneered a new philosophy, but as the act was administered over the succeeding years it became a very conservative type of operation where loans were only made on the basis of a farmer's assets. The potential profit of money put toward new productivity was not considered. It simply acted like a bank. If a man had $10,000 worth of assets, he might take out a loan of $4,000. Very few risks were taken and there was very little development of new technology under that philosophy.
The philosophy of the 1959 legislation was to consider the potential profit if a man were loaned $10,000, $20,000 or $30,000, and if the loan were put to proper use. Therefore, people began working on the Farm Credit Corporation with

the farmer, out of the various provincial branches, to get a plan ready. Their philosophy was that if the farmer spent his money, it would increase his income, not only enabling him to pay back his debt but also leaving a nice, handsome net gain for the farmer during the repayment period.
That legislation was conditional on the power of the government of the day to persuade those who worked for the new Farm Credit Corporation to change their philosophy of lending on assets, not caring a hoot what the farmer did with the money so long as he could pay it back, to one of trying to help the farmer increase his growth and productivity, which would benefit the whole country. The Farm Credit Corporation grew and expanded on that basis. However, recently, in the last ten or 12 years, I have noticed a reversal of philosophy by those administering farm credit. Only ten or 15 years ago when I spoke to the Farm Credit Corporation people they were very willing to lend money for cattle, although they had decided there was a need for more livestock in the country. Because of this philosophy, it was very easy to get loans if one wanted to expand one's cattle operation, but it was not so easy to get loans for other purposes. 1 do not blame the Farm Credit Corporation people for that. Maybe they called the shot right.
As we know now, of course, the cattle industry overexpanded, and we have been suffering pretty well ever since. However, that should not be held against the Farm Credit Corporation because it was doing what it thought would give the greatest potential to that farmer.
I will not go through all the details, but 1 have now said enough that 1 must ask the following question: If that was the philosophy of the act which was in existence in 1959, what is the philosophy which is coming through in this bill and amendment? It seems to me that the philosophy coming out now is that the only people who will get money from the Farm Credit Corporation are those who need it the most. If you are doing well today as a farmer and want to do better, you cannot get money from the Farm Credit Corporation. It tells the farmer that he is doing all right and can get his own money. It sounds good politically for the government to say it wants to help the guy who needs it the most.
Under the philosophy of the Farm Credit Corporation there is no use lending money to a farmer if he will not be able to pay back the loan and if he will not be able to increase his income. The philosophy of potential growth must be in there.
We heard the figures from the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) a moment ago. Even in a tough year like 1979-80, all the corporation had was a million dollars worth of losses on one year's lending in a large portfolio across the country. The point I am making is that this tips me off that if you have small losses for your lending on potential, it either means the country is growing so fast that you cannot make a mistake or that the government is changing its philosophy to one of not lending money unless it gets it back.
When I hear this talk about studies for farmers in severe economic circumstances, or dire straits as the phrase goes, I
Farm Loans
begin to suspect that we have gone right back to the old handout philosophy of the old farm loan board of 1934. In those days, when a farmer went to a farm loan board after his first few years of operation, he went there to get help because he was in trouble. He found it very difficult to receive help when he was in difficulty because the board reviewed his assets. It was concerned, as a Conservative should be, about his ability to pay it back. But the new Conservative government of 1959 changed that philosophy. Its philosophy was to look at a farmer's plans to make money and give him all he needed to increase his income. We did not intend to lose money, but were prepared to lose it if the plan did not work.
I say that the history of the growth rate of agriculture in Canada over the last 20 years demonstrates that the philosophy of 1959 did work with minimal losses. In fact, the Farm Credit Corporation showed a profit over the years.
I detect now that the Farm Credit Corporation is going back to that old civil service concept that all the federal government should do is to look after those people who cannot get money from other sources. The government has become a lender of last resort.
The philosophy that we put in the act, which I helped to draft in 1959, was that we did not care about being a lender of last resort. We wanted the Farm Credit Corporation to advertise across the country that we had money to lend for people with ideas to make more money. That was the philosophy of that day. As minister for three years in charge of that act, my concern was that with this past background of the civil service which would be administering this new act, it would revert back to the old farm loan mentality. I think that my suspicions were right.
For the First number of years its philosophy did change. However, I detected over this last ten or 13 years when I talked to people in my own constituency that the philosophy was changing. Now, budding young farmers and successful middle-aged farmers do not go to the Farm Credit Corporation any more. They know they will be turned down because they are successful. The FCC, under the act now, is not supposed to be a lender of last resort. The philosophy was to back up winners. There are all sorts of winners, poor and rich. I would go further to say that I think the greatest mistake I made as minister was not to have put in clear legislative form that if a man had potential, we did not care what his assets were. A young farmer, if he had a program that would make money, whether he wanted $100,000 or $200,000, could get it even without assets.
Today, however, when the government lends money under the Farm Credit Corporation, it tries to tie down all the borrower's relatives and neighbours. We have a situation today in which a man who tries to get a loan through the Farm Credit Corporation must be backed by his uncle on the next farm for a certain proportion. Now his uncle cannot retire until this young farmer has paid off the debt. All this land is tied up and all the prospects for these farmers to retire are tied up. This is cruel.

Other governments have tried this. There was the young farmers loans legislation in Ontario from 1948 to 1959. Only a few thousand dollars was lost, and money was lent without regard to assets. All a farmer had to have was the approval of the local county board. If the board said he was a good, hardworking person, that was all that was required in assets.

All we have to do is to look at the financial records of that American legislation. They were backing a man's potential, and that is the greatest asset in the world. My question to the House is simple. Having heard this debate and having heard the different views expressed by the minister and other hon. members that these housekeeping reforms are necessary, let hon. members ask themselves the question; in all honesty, has the philosophy changed in the Farm Credit Corporation? It does not matter to me whether there are five members on the board or 15. Has the philosophy stayed the same? 1 suspect that it has not.
I will use one major example. This is why I am glad the minister is here. He knows that many of us have been concerned about the Farm Credit Corporation. Personally, I have not been concerned about the supply of money as have many others. I am concerned about the philosophy. To make sure there was no question about the lack of money, several members in the Conservative Party got up last year and suggested that we use the principle of the Small Business Development Bond for the Farm Credit Corporation. It was suggested that the act be amended to allow this corporation to accept money from any person but, hopefully, from farmers in particular who would put their spare cash into the Farm Credit Corporation which would receive an interest rate at maybe 8 per cent, knowing that when they got that 8 per cent interest they would not be taxed on it. I alone am not responsible for this idea. I did make it too. But there was the hon. member for Medicine Hat, (Mr. Hargrave), the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton), the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), the hon. member for Fethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) and many others-if I missed them I am sorry-as well as members on the other side, and the minister himself, who gave their approval to this idea. I remember the minister giving approval to this idea on television and I was hopeful that if it could be used as a principle-as it was used in the Clark-Crosbie budget of 1979-and if it was being renewed again, this principle in Farm Credit with all its machinery here, with all
its capital allowance, then let it draw its capital from many sources as well as from the government.
The government has gone out and borrowed money at 19.5 per cent. It rightfully feels that it cannot just turn money over to any industry at much less than that. It is turning it over at a little bit less to the Farm Credit Corporation. But let the public come in, let anybody come in, and lend on a Small Business Development Bond, knowing it is not going to be taxable, and it is quite content to take 8 per cent on non-taxable lending. You can show no one is subsidizing anyone because the farmer who gets his money at half interest rates, such as 9Vi, loses his right for deductions when he pays that interest. So the government wins on that one. If the government loses, it is not collecting the tax on the 8 per cent of the lending, but looking at it fairly and objectively, no one is subsidizing anyone.
There will be academic arguments that there is a tax expenditure here, but no one but a nitwit would ever use that expression because the reality is that no one is subsidizing anyone. The government is not hurting its balance of ways and means because if the loan is not made, it will not get any money anyway.
The main thing here was that people from all parties were behind the minister on that proposal. I could say similar things to what I understood the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) to say, but a similar suggestion has been made for housing. I was dreadfully disappointed when I heard that budget on November 12. After approval was obtained and the minister stuck his neck out and supported the proposal, I was very disappointed that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) did not bring it forward in his budget.
I wonder what would happen if we in this House moved an amendment to this legislation proposing, in simple layman's form, that this should be done. We are not asking the government for any expenditure of money, so I think it would be acceptable under the rules. If we had the support of the Minister of Agriculture, the government would be very embarrassed if it did not accept the amendment. I would like to get a reaction to that proposal because we do not have much more time to wait. High interest rates are killing everybody, including the farmer, and no farmer in his right mind should ever borrow money, even at 16% per cent. All parties could support it. It would put the government in a fantastic position. It would not dare say we are costing it any money. We would not have offended the rules of Parliament. We would be carrying out something the people need and want. At the same time we could show

Mr. Speaker, It is with great pleasure that I take part in this debate on farm loans. [English]
Not so many years ago credit and mortgages were not subjects easily discussed by farmers. Most of them felt it was a matter of pride to pay cash and not to borrow money. Of course, many of these people had witnessed the ravages of the depression, and they remembered a friend or neighbour who had lost his farm through foreclosure.
When we look back in history, and in particular the history of the Farm Credit Corporation, we find that its predecessor, the Canadian farm loan board, came into existence because farmers did not have access to an adequate source of credit. Agriculture has not changed all that much over the years. Farmers still have to contend with the vagaries of our climate. Even if we have developed better and hardier varieties, insects and weeds continue to be a problem. Adequate returns to ensure a profitable business operation continue to be one of the main concerns of most farmers.
The government is concerned about the difficulties farmers face because their fate is intimately linked to that of every Canadian citizen and many of our foreign buyers. Farmers provide the vital foodstuff to sustain life.
If agriculture has been as successful an industry as it has, it is because of the determination and ingenuity of Canadian farmers. The role government has played and must continue to play, in my opinion, is that of a supporter and facilitator. There are numerous examples of this, from the extensive research programs provided by Agriculture Canada to the stabilization programs and the inspection services offered.
I wish to concentrate my comments on what I consider to be one of the essential tools of today's farm business credit. Credit has been one of the true catalysts in the growth of Canadian agriculture. When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) speaks of the efficiency of the family farm and the Canadian farmer, he is simply reaffirming the facts which are there for all to see.
The credit tool government has created to help farmers is the Farm Credit Corporation. In its 22 years of existence it has assisted some 160,000 borrowers. The minister mentioned in his remarks that 74,000 of these borrowers still have loans outstanding with the FCC.
In terms of the economy it is difficult to measure what the FCC contributes to Canada by financing the development of viable farming operations. Although the nominal benefits to the economy are difficult to assess, some measurements are possible.
Facilitating the transfer from generation to generation of farms and providing capital investment in farming are considered essential to the long-term productivity and stability of the agricultural sector. These are necessary if the agri-food
Farm Loans
sector is to continue to provide Canadian consumers with an abundant supply of high quality food at a reasonable price, as well as provide for the export market which contributes so significantly to our balance of payments. The corporation strongly supports the family farm as the major means of food production. In 1979-80 and 1980-81, close to 98 per cent of all loans approved were to family farms.
In 1980-81, FCC borrowers increased their farm operating expenditures an estimated $100 million because of farm expansion, capital improvements and other agricultural investment projects. These increased annual expenditures, combined with credit extended by the FCC, contribute considerably to the economic health and growth of rural communities and agricultural service industries.
The success of FCC borrowers reflects their contribution to agricultural productivity levels and therefore to the Canadian economy. In recent years, the FCC has had to turn away a good number of applicants because of its shortage of capital. Data indicates that 65 per cent of those applicants who were declined loans because of their strong financial position had previously received FCC loans. Data on 2,622 borrowers whose loans in 1980-81 were assumed or retired indicates that over 91 per cent were considered successful. In addition, 93 per cent of all 72,663 accounts were in good standing as of March 31, 1981. This proves beyond doubt, in my mind, that farmers have more than lived up to the faith placed in them by the Canadian government.
An analysis of the effectiveness of the Farm Credit Corporation which was conducted last year indicates that the FCC is playing a significant role in facilitating the development of viable farm operations and thus contributing to the Canadian economy. Furthermore, the results of a special FCC survey of farmers which was completed in 1981 show that the corporation is currently lending to a much smaller scale of farm than the average. This substantiates our belief that the role of government in the financing of Canadian farmers is more important than ever, in spite of the greater share which private institutions have taken in the long-term agricultural lending market during the last five years.
The federal government's participation through the FCC has been reduced from over two thirds of this market to less than one quarter, primarily due to limited capital resources. During this period, the chartered banks and credit unions, as well as the provincial government in some provinces, particularly Alberta, Quebec and Nova Scotia, have lent substantial amounts in the long-term lending field. But in times of economic difficulties or when larger returns can be earned elsewhere, many of these institutions direct their funds elsewhere. The stability in supply of credit must be assured for all farmers who are efficient and productive.
The FCC's contribution has been essential to farm stability in many periods of difficulty because it provided mortgages with an attractive rate fixed for a period of up to 30 years,

when private institutions could only offer long-term credit with variable interest rates.
Also, the corporation strives to provide loans to those applicants who have viable proposals but who do not meet or who would have difficulty in meeting the security or repayment criteria required by the private sector. The FCC will continue to provide credit for these higher risk borrowers, not for those who have access to commercial sources of financing.
Since FCC was given the authority to make loans up to 100 per cent of the value of the security in 1975, the trend has been to loans with less security. In many situations, additional security is not available, which is typical of young beginning farmers, and the corporation does not hesitate to take higher risks than other lending institutions would. I wish to repeat the percentage which has been quoted: in recent years some 70 per cent of FCC loans has been going to young borrowers under 35 years of age.
Furthermore, FCC authorizes some of its borrowers to defer their payments until other pressures on their cash flow subside, and this probably means survival for these farmers.
In spite of its restricted budget, the corporation has been able to keep in close contact with the Canadian farming community. Farmers, although they know FCC has less money to lend, continue to approach the FCC officers for advice and farm management counselling. This is the kind of strength which is essential to a wise use of credit. The FCC plays a major role in this educational process.
In the 1980-81 fiscal year, 204 credit advisers in 103 field offices gave more than 47,000 interviews in the selection of loan applicants or the administration of loan accounts. A total of 27,409 specific loan requests were received. After assessment of these requests, 4,686 loans for a total of $508.9 million were approved. Some 17 per cent of all loan requests were approved. Of the 23 per cent of the loans declined at the interview stage, 32 per cent were declined because of insufficient repayment potential, 30 per cent had the resources and repayment potential to get credit elsewhere, 16 per cent were not planning to become principally occupied in farming and 22 per cent were declined for other reasons.
Although five out of six loan requests were declined, only 121 of these decisions were appealed by farmers. In most cases, credit advisers were able to provide applicants with alternatives to further their farm development plans.
I could go on for some time expounding the positive role played by the FCC in its lending program, but I wish to conclude by giving credit where it is due, to the farmer. We must remember that the borrower repays the funds borrowed. Farm Credit is an investment for the Canadian government, not a gift or a handout.
Are there farmers in your riding?

Yes, we do have farmers in the riding. Farmers pay their own way. I trust we will continue to demonstrate our faith in their ability by providing our Canadian farmers with a good supply of the much needed tool that
credit is. These amendments provide a starting point for interesting new developments in this field.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in considering Bill C-88, an act respecting loans to farmers which was introduced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and received first reading in the House on January 27, we see that its purpose is to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow supplemental funding on the private marketplace; to enact the interest rate rebate provision of the budget; to increase the board of directors from five to seven members, to remove the 35-year-old age limitation on Section 33 loans; and to update some of the language of the Farm Credit Act.
For over a year the Minister of Agriculture has stated that such legislation would soon be introduced, so we are delighted to see it finally in front of us. He took his time, of course. We had legislation similar to this in the planning stages in the latter days of our government, some two years ago.
Farm groups have generally been supportive of this legislation, as long as it is supplemental funding and not a replacement of government funding. We basically support this legislation, provided that the government does not intend to cut back on its financial commitment to the Farm Credit Corporation.
For other than patronage reasons we question the need for the board to be expanded to seven members, as has been mentioned by many of my colleagues. We also believe that the Farm Credit Corporation should be provided with an additional $500 million. It is interesting to note that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has called for an additional $1 billion. This legislation will not solve the short-term underfunding problem of the Farm Credit Corporation. This extra $50 million in the budget is not sufficient.
As members on this side of the House who spoke previously have indicated, we support the legislation. What we do not support is the inaction of the Liberal government opposite, especially as it relates to the agricultural sector in Canada. The food producing sector in Canada is not receiving the priority it merits. When we view some of the figures published by Statistics Canada, we find that bankruptcies increased close to 50 per cent this year compared to last. We also find in this disastrous budget which was introduced on November 12- which will have a disastrous effect on the farming population of Canada- that the provisions regarding the income-averaging annuity contracts as they pertain to the agricultural sector are disastrous. The capital gains provisions as announced and consequently amended will also be disastrous for the agricultural sector.
The part of all this that is most detrimental is the lack of any action relating to interest rates. The reduction in the capital cost allowance in the November 12 budget means that farmers buying equipment will now pay substantially more income tax in the first year. This is the view of the Manitoba agriculture farm management specialist, Irwin Wiebe.
February 1, 1982

The Minister of Agriculture has made a mockery of his portfolio, Mr. Speaker. He has lost credibility throughout the land, and I will share the reason for that with you. On many occasions when he was speaking to farm groups, we have heard the minister indicate that he felt the banks were making far too much profit. He has indicated this repeatedly throughout Canada. He has blamed the banks for the high interest rate situation. Yet on two occasions in the chamber when he had an opportunity to do something about it, he voted against imposing an excess profits tax on the banking industry. On January 26, 1982, a motion proposing that we put an excess profits tax on the banking industry was voted against by the Minister of Agriculture. That action, as well as many of his other actions, shows that the minister is truly making a mockery of his responsibilities.
Because of a lack of action on the part of the national government, the provinces have been required to introduce programs on their own relating to the hog and beef industry. We require in Canada a comprehensive national program as it relates to both the beef and hog industry. Recently the province of Alberta introduced a cattle and sheep program because of the inaction of the minister opposite. Also, it is interesting to note that last year when the minister made his initial announcement pertaining to the hog industry, he was not going to make any payment to Alberta. After a great deal of lobbying by various farm groups, he changed his mind and introduced some fairness into the hog stabilization program.
1 travelled throughout my constituency during the Christmas recess, visiting such areas as Newbrook and Westlock. Residents of those areas indicated a deep concern about the survival of the Canadian agricultural sector and about the lack of action on the part of the present Liberal administration. When we were in government, we took specific steps to aid the Canadian agricultural sector. We were in the process of working with various provincial governments to establish national programs, so that each province would not have to initiate its own program to the detriment of all. We had hoped that the Small Business Development Bond would have been of more use to the farm sector in that farmers could use them at reduced interest rates for expansion purposes. We introduced specific capital gains relief for the farming sector to the tune of some $200,000. When one looks at the record of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Manzankowski) when he was minister of transport, one sees that we shipped record amounts of grain as well.
There are few sectors of the economy which are as dependent upon borrowed money as in agriculture. Farmers require money to start their operations and to remain in business. Most of their costs are fixed, which reduces any flexibility in times of financial crisis. When farmers hurt, so does the rural community. Recent figures show that businesses throughout the rural community, business investment and business turnover in terms of cash flow, has dropped in the vicinity of some 50 per cent.
Farm Loans
The government should adopt a number of ideas to help Canadian farmers. 1 should like to share with the minister a number of points which should be adopted that would be of great help to the farming sector. We should introduce a moratorium on farm bankruptcies, foreclosures and forced sales to allow the government time to enact more meaningful assistance for farmers. We should have an infusion of some $500 million into the Farm Credit Corporation to subsidize interest rates and increase loan programs for farmers. We should create a committee, including farm representatives, to monitor the Small Business Development Bond program and to help save unincorporated farmers from bankruptcy. We should allow farmers to use the Small Business Development Bond to build and to expand their operations, rather than it being used by only those in dire straits. There should be the payment of a subsidy to farmers faced with interest rates of over 12 per cent on loans taken out for less than ten years. There should be enactment of the Liberal promise of the 1980 election campaign to change valuation day for capital gains tax on farmland from 1971 to 1974. The minister cannot even live up to that promise he made to the agricultural sector. It is my feeling that the capital gains tax provision should be abolished completely as it relates to the agricultural sector. There should also be a rebate on the price of fuel used in food production. There should be a national price stabilization plan for beef and for hogs, which is a meaningful plan, rather than the ad hoc plan that leaves far too much discretion in the minister's hands.
We offered that in 1977.
1 hope the minister will take the opportunity to respond to a number of concerns we have raised.
Given the opportunity, I will.

We will give the minister the opportunity as long as he promises to be more credible in his answers than he was when he indicated that the banks should do away with their excess profits. Agriculture could be radically changed in the next three to five years if no action is taken. This is extremely bad news for all Canada, especially Canadian farmers, consumers, businessmen, and labour groups.
Bill C-88 should be an important and worth-while measure in the long-range funding of the Farm Credit Corporation. As I indicated earlier, we will support this legislation, provided the government gives a firm commitment that its direct funding to the FCC will not be cut back. I ask the minister to respond by giving us a commitment that the federal government will not cut back on its funding. Also, we hope that the government will guarantee the bonds floated by the Farm Credit Corporation so that they could be sold more quickly. We all look forward to a more detailed study of this legislation when it is referred to committee.
In closing I should like to put another question to the minister. Are there any plans in regard to the PFRA? There have been a number of suggestions by hon. members on this side of the House that it should be redirected and put under

February 1, 1982
Farm Loans
Agriculture Canada rather than under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I hope the minister will give this matter serious consideration, as we did when we examined the possibility when the responsibility fell under the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). Also I suggest that this plan should be expanded upon so as to become a national program rather than a regional one.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is a well known fact that the production of food requires proper and modern tools, if we are to maintain the high quality and standards that have been achieved over a number of years in the production of excellent food, not only for Canadians but for consumers all over the world. Also it is a well-known fact that one of those proper tools is proper financing. The fact that the Farm Credit Corporation bill is being debated in the House and will be referred to committee later is very welcome.
1 feel somewhat sorry for some of the field workers of the Farm Credit Corporation who, for the last year or 18 months, have had inadequate funds to meet the needs of the areas they represent. Many times loan applications have been refused. Even the refusal to take applications from applicants makes it very difficult for individuals in those offices; they see a need but, because of a lack of financing, loans are not possible at the time, or at any time for that matter.
In July, August or September of last year it appeared that there were no funds left to lend out at a somewhat lesser rate than that of today, that is, in the area of 14 per cent. This was mainly because representatives of the FCC indicated that all funds were being held until the new rate was set. Subsequently, a new rate was established at 16.75 per cent, and since budget time some loans were approved. The budget included a provision wherein there would be a reduction of 5 per cent on farm credit loans to 11.75 per cent. At the present time, some young farmers are starting out, saddled with the 16.75 per cent interest rate tied to the mortgages on their land for the next 29 or 30 years. Suddenly, the next few years are very important for those young people who find it difficult to make a living in agriculture, with the structure of their land base and getting established. It would only be proper if some subsidization were given them, especially those young people who were "fortunate" enough to obtain mortgages even at 16.75 per cent.
In Poland today meat prices have risen some 300 per cent. Pork chops rose from 60 cents a pound to $3 per pound. If we are not careful and do not maintain a good strong agricultural base here in Canada, it is possible that we could be facing the same situation. Consumers will have to pay extremely high prices for food if we do not provide the proper tools to agriculture now. It might be too late now. We know that we will lose many of our small farmers, those young farmers who started farming within the last six or seven years. Many of them started out with very little money. I am a farmer. I started with all borrowed money. I borrowed from my father
to make my start. If it had not been for my father, I would not have been able to farm, even though it was very difficult for him to assist me at that time.
The bill we have here today is actually two pieces of legislation, and one wonders why the government has scheduled so much legislation for transmittal to the Standing Committee on Agriculture all at the same time. Certainly this committee has been fumbling around doing almost nothing for most of the past two years, and now suddenly we have debated three measures in a week for reference to it.
I am tempted to ask whether the government is scheduling its agriculture legislation in this way in order to push Cana-grex through without much scrutiny, or whether it is shoving farm credit legislation through right behind the Canagrex bill in order to deflect attention away from the severe problems farmers have been facing while waiting and waiting for an improvement to farm credit Financing.
There are some measures in the present legislation that will be welcome to our food producers that we on this side of the House will certainly want to support. For example, an increase in the capital of the Farm Credit Corporation is very much needed and will do a great deal to stabilize the financing of land in the Canadian agricultural industry. That is, it will do so once the problems raised by this bill are worked out.
Farm credit has been underfunded for years now, and as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) indicated the other day, he has been relying on the private banks to pick up the slack since 1975. We have all seen in the past two years how poorly they did the job of managing farm financing. In some cases, the banks employed personnel who knew far too little about agriculture to be in the business of agricultural lending. In other cases, the banks used poor judgment in matching the type of loan they were offering to the kind of asset or operation being financed. Much of this sloppiness on the part of the banks might have gone unnoticed if it were not for the monstrous fluctuations in interest rates which have been brought on by this government's policy of high interest rates. The Minister of Agriculture may want to blame the banks for writing lending contracts that allowed them to convert what should have been mortgages into demand loans, but the truth is that the policies of this government are too erratic and arbitrary for the banks to use a straight mortgage instrument to handle all kinds of farm financing.
It is the policy of the government to which the minister belongs that has caused much of the present problem. I hope the minister has now learned a lesson that he can teach to his cabinet colleagues, namely, to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to do what it was set up to do, that is, to finance the long-term assets of land and buildings which make possible family farming in Canada. In particular, I hope the minister is now committed to the idea that the Farm Credit Corporation is the proper vehicle for helping new farmers establish themselves in business.
That, Mr. Speaker, is what this legislation should be all about. I believe legislation to increase the Farm Credit Corporation's capital has been ready for two years. Better late than
February 1, 1982

never, perhaps, but let us note that too late means never, and for many hundreds of Canadians who were and who wanted to be farmers, this legislation has come too late. It is important now that the assistance contained in this legislation be provided as soon as possible. But clearly, the difficulties surrounding this piece of legislation have not yet been worked out. For that reason, the sooner the bill gets to committee and the committee gets down to serious examination of it, the better. I, for one, hope that the Standing Committee on Agriculture has the opportunity to give immediate attention to this bill, and is not delayed and obstructed in its job by red herrings such as a supposed need to get Canagrex operating by the middle of next week.
Let us note how helpful this present bill could be in theory. One of its principal effects would be to raise the capital of the Farm Credit Corporation by $75 million, thereby raising the amount the Farm Credit Corporation could borrow and lend out again by $1,875 billion. This is a very significant amount.
Another principal effect is to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow from private sources some of the money it borrows on the basis of its authorized capital.
The minister the other day, in introducing this legislation, mentioned pension funds as one possible source of such borrowed funds, and then raised the possibility of allowing retiring farmers to provide another source through some plan equivalent to the small business bond plan by which banks can lend money at little more than half the prevailing interest rate. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) had a grasp of what fiscal management means, he might see his way clear to bringing in this kind of measure so it becomes more than a possibility.
At the moment, the Minister of Finance seems to regard money as being of two types. One, the type he has lound is a way to take by way of taxes. Second, a type he is still trying to get hold of. If he could grasp that there are ways to put money to work so that both he as the tax grabber and other Canadians as producers could have more to play with, he would have advanced a long way toward helping the economy achieve its potential.
One idea he might well consider is the one his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, has now seen the wisdom of, namely, allowing retiring farmers to invest funds with the Farm Credit Corporation as a way to reduce their tax burden. But this matter is one not for debate at the present time. It deserves full examination, and perhaps now that we on this side of the House have recruited the Minister of Agriculture to adopt it, we can encourage the Minister of Finance to see that it serves his interests too.
At present, the Farm Credit Corporation can borrow up to 25 times its capital out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to lend out. The new bill would authorize the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow 25 times its increased capital, but it would no longer be required to borrow only from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. It would now also be able to raise money on the private markets. In theory, the addition of $75
Adjournment Dehate
million to the authorized capital of the Farm Credit Corporation should allow the corporation to raise an additional $1,875 billion in private borrowing. Certainly, an additional amount like this of almost $2 billion would be more than enough to meet the present needs of Canadian agriculture. Of course, in practice, things do not work this way. Each year, the Farm Credit Corporation receives a certain portion of its capital from the government and then proceeds to borrow up to 25 times that amount from the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-ENTITLEMENT TO RETROACTIVE PENSION PAYMENTS
VETERANS AFFAIRS-ENTITLEMENT TO RETROACTIVE PENSION PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I directed a question to the Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs this afternoon. I pointed out that close to 4,000 veterans receiving less than 5 per cent disability pensions have never been informed that they are eligible for a yearly consumer price index increase on a little known final payment allotment. I understand that some of these veterans are on the computer system and receive this entitlement but we do not know how many have been left off that system. Entitlement of final payment exists for veterans who have been given a disability pension of from 1 per cent to 4 per cent. Four thousand veterans are eligible for yearly consumer price increases on an original payment of $100. The problem is that they must apply for these or they will not receive them. In some cases they may have over $1,000 in back pay coming to them. Why is payment not automatically made? Will all veterans in this category be informed of this and paid retroactively, and what about future payments? To date there appears to be utter confusion in this category.
In addition, veterans will be penalized further under the Liberal budget. Resolution 53 of the budget will cost them thousands of dollars a year. The Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs today in question period misled the House when he

February 1, 1982
Adjournment Debate
stated there are no provisions in the budget which would affect veterans. The budget will make veterans' pensions calculable income, something which has never been done in the past.
A veteran's working spouse may claim a veteran as a dependant only if he makes less than $3,660 in any year. This will most certainly eliminate tens of thousands of currently eligible veterans, thus cancelling the spouse's deduction. It will have the effect of drastically reducing a veteran family's net income, putting them on the tax man's firing line.
We are still having problems with widows' pension applications. Administration is slow. The process was supposed to take place immediately on passage of Bill C-82, but there are still widows who have been waiting for many months. As an example, a constituent of mine, whose husband died December 13, 1980, applied for a widow's pension in January, 1981. The application was never acknowledged by the department. In August, 1981, seven months later, she received a letter telling her to apply if she had not already done so. My office was informed early in January, 1982, that the pension had been granted, and contacted her with the news. She also received a letter from the pension commission dated January 6, 1982, saying that she would be receiving a proportionate pension. The total time from the original application was one year. The total time from the letter asking for the application was five months. So you see the problem we still have there, Mr. Speaker.
Now, there are many problems facing veterans which have been made perfectly clear by the Public Accounts Committee in its tenth report; the Senate committee report "They Served, We Care;" Legion submissions; the Auditor General's report; the Hong Kong Veterans Association; National Indian Veterans Association; and repeated representations from the Conservative Party. The problems are never ending.
We also have the prisoner of war benefit discrepancies which have not been settled, with no statement from the minister. The amount of interest income which can be exempted from federal taxes is now a mere $100 and should be raised to $1,000, but we hear nothing from the department.
There is next to no value in the aging veterans' programs. For example, only 92 vetrans are currently eligible for the home support program across Canada. It is far too restrictive. There are inequities which divorced spouses must face when they receive no entitlement under the pension act and the War Veterans Allowance Act. There are also the inequities in the way veterans are compensated for time spent as prisoners of war. We have these persistent unremedied time delays which were condemned by the Public Accounts Committee when it said they should be replaced by a time limit of 180 days for the entire process. Now we have this cruel budget provision which will in effect tax veterans' families when they cannot even survive on their current levels of income. The question is, Mr. Speaker, when will the minister resolve these mounting problems?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-ENTITLEMENT TO RETROACTIVE PENSION PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague on the other side of the House raised about 12 different issues. I realize that I have only about three minutes in which to respond, so perhaps I could address only two of those issues. Specifically, I would like to address his question with respect to the final payment types of pensions. Perhaps "final payment" is not the proper description. These are annual payments which are made to veterans who have been awarded assessments of 5 per cent or less.
In 1921, when the legislation was introduced, there was provision that anyone receiving a pension under 5 per cent would receive a single payment versus a monthly payment. Between 1921 and 1971 eight adjustments were made to those single payment pensions. In 1972, the CPI was introduced, and the same thing has applied to pensions of this type as pensions on a monthly basis. The CPI has automatically been applied and has been applied all the way through.
For example, in 1973, there was a 24 per cent increase in the base rate for these types of pensions. The CPI has been applied all the way through. Just to give a classic example, since January 1, 1982, when the 12.3 per cent was announced, there has been an adjustment in the single payment, or "final payment" as it is known, of 1,246 pensions. A further 2,654 will be processed just as quickly as possible. We hope that by the end of February all the single payment pensioners will be receiving the adjustment. They have received this treatment all the way through, and they will continue to do so.
The hon. member is quite correct. Approximately 4,000 have been receiving their cost of living adjustment, as has been the case for the duration of their pensions. However, before I wind up, I want to address a question which I thought the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) resolved the other day with respect to the application of the budget to veterans.
Under resolution 53, there is a provision for prescribed programs. I want to say to the House and to the veterans of Canada that the programs under Veterans Affairs, the disability pensions and the War Veterans Allowance, will continue to be exempted from the application of the budget and, specifically, from the requirement to take these provisions into income in tax calculations. That was made clear the other day, and I want to reinforce that fact. Under resolution 53, which was cited by the hon. member, "prescribed" and "exempted" programs under veterans affairs will continue to enjoy the same decision with respect to the programs of the Government of Canada they have enjoyed in the past.
