speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question tonight asks for further illumination on a question I directed in the House to the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) on November 9, 1981. At that time, I
February 1, 1982

indicated to the minister that I had in my hand a letter the minister had received from the Canadian Council of Churches, requesting a policy change in Canada's relations with El Salvador and Canada's view of El Salvador. At that time, I also had a letter from the Canadian Catholic Bishops which stated that the military and Christian Democratic ruling junta in El Salvador is responsible, before its own nation and before the international community, for extremely grave crimes.
At the same time, 1 asked a supplementary question of the hon. minister, regarding the UPI meetings in Havana which had proceeded during that summer. The Chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, along with a group of parliamentarians from Canada, had voted at those meetings to support the French-Mexican position. At that time, the minister told me that the initiative was largely discredited and that Canada would not change its position regarding elections to be held in El Salvador. These elections have been called, as everyone knows. In light of that fact, I continue my question with this new information.
On December 8 the subcommittee on External Affairs dealing with relations between Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean, of which I am a member, brought its report to this House. In it we indicated that the situation in El Salvador demands a pre-electoral period of political negotiation and stability. I quote:
While the subcommittee has no illusions about the ease of achieving these conditions, we think they consist of three essential elements: first, serious negotiations between all parties to the conflict; second, an internationally supervised cease-fire; third, and only after the achievement of these conditions an internationally supervised electoral process in El Salvador.
That report of the subcommittee was unanimously voted on by members of all three parties in this House.
During the Christmas recess there were several delegations which went to the area of El Salvador. One delegation, under the auspices of Oxfam Canada, made up of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) and the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) visited refugees from El Salvador in refugee camps in the Honduras.
On their return, they said quite emphatically that the possibility of elections in El Salvador is a myth. They cannot take place. There cannot be a truly democratic election at this time.
This past week I and several members of the subcommittee on Latin American and Caribbean relations were in the Central American area. In company with the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki), I visited a refugee camp of El Salvadoran refugees in Costa Rica near the Honduran border. From that information, and from information received from literally all other sources, during our visit, it appears to us that the report we handed down in December is accurate and that at this time the elections that are called to take place in El Salvador are an impossibility. There are over
Adjournment Debate
600,000	refugees inside and outside the country, most of them naturally being in the opposition.
In the Catholic Register of January 30, there is a story from San Salvador which speaks of the recent position of Bishop Arturo Rivera Damas, the acting apostolic administrator of the diocese of San Salvador. In this article in which he asks the people of El Salvador to reflect on his belief, he states:
the conflict of El Salvador is at the heart of the east-west conflict and runs the risk of becoming truly international with no end in sight
We address the guerrilla fighters themselves to ponder their actions in light of a national, patriotic outlook and not under alien influence,... We ask all political parties, all those responsible for the public administration to look at our situation with a realistic approach, devoid of ideological passions, and find political solutions that can lead to peace.
I do not want to set up a conflict with the government or the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but in light of this information 1 have given tonight, in addition to my previous question, 1 plead that the government take a new and serious look at the situation.
In the trip which the committee completed yesterday to the Caribbean and Central America, we found, and I can state this emphatically, that Canada has a very high and good profile in that whole area. I suggest that profile is far out of proportion to what we have done in that area. Canada does not have an imperialistic past there. People look to us as being just, and of those who will help.
During our trip inside El Salvador, in the past few weeks, we met journalists, including journalists from the Miami Herald, who indicated from their observations that, having talked with the guerrillas and as a result of the escalation of the war which took place last week when military aircraft were destroyed, and also from talking to the government people, much to my surprise they believe the Duarte government will actually lose the election. They will lose the election to extreme forces to the right because anybody who represents the middle, which is practically non-existent, or leftist forces, will not be there to vote.
In the light of this new information, and in the light of what I hope is the true, sincere and just feelings of our government, I would like to further my question by asking if the government is ready to re-evaluate its position on the question of El Salvador; to take positive steps, some of which were suggested in my question of November 9, in opening up our embassy and calling together the forces of various disputing parties; of going out of our way and taking the extra step of using our good profile, that good feeling we have in that part of the world, to call upon those forces to come together in negotiation and not to set up an election which can only lead to more disruptive situations in that very volatile part of the world.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-ENTITLEMENT TO RETROACTIVE PENSION PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Canada's position on El Salvador has been expressed many times, notably in statements in the House of Commons by the Secretary of State for

February 1, 1982
Adjournment Debate
External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). Canada is opposed to foreign intervention in the domestic affairs of El Salvador and believes that the problem of El Salvador must be resolved by El Salvadorans without foreign interference. Canada has a long-standing policy of not providing arms to areas of tension and deplores the fact that competing forces in El Salvador are receiving supplies from outside sources.
Canada hopes the dialogue on a political solution in El Salvador would encompass all political parties and welcomes the expressed willingness of the government of El Salvador to enter into dialogue on the electoral process with opposition groups willing to lay down their arms.
The Canadian government is not at this time prepared to associate itself with the declaration made on August 28, 1981, by the governments of France and Mexico because it believes that the appropriate political solution is through the electoral process rather than through negotiations. Canada would also be willing to provide technical assistance for the electoral process and to consider participation in international observation of the elections.
We are now discussing with the El Salvador authorities various aspects of the proposed election and observation process so as to determine the nature of the Canadian response. It is not for Canada or Canadians to support or oppose El Salvador's decision to have elections though persons and governments are entitled to their individual views.
It is the government's view that President Duarte should be commended for his efforts to hold democratic elections in very difficult circumstances and we hope that all political parties in that country will respond to his government's invitation to participate.
With regard to the question of human rights in El Salvador, the Secretary of State for External Affairs clearly indicated in his statement in the House on June 16 that the government is very sensitive to and concerned about the human rights situation in El Salvador. Those concerns have been expressed to the government of El Salvador and to representatives of the FLMN/FDR. Like all Canadians, the government deplores the senseless killing which has occurred in El Salvador these past many months, killing which has been perpetrated by both sides in that tragic conflict.
We are particularly disturbed by news reports today of a tragic shooting incident in San Salvador. We immediately called in the Charge d'Affaires of the Embassy of El Salvador to express our concern and to request him to obtain from his government a clarification as to the exact circumstances of the incident. We also instructed our ambassador to El Salvador, resident in Costa Rica, to obtain similar clarification.
It has been reported that the United States is considering the supply of new helicopters to replace those recently destroyed by insurgent forces in El Salvador. Our position on the supply of arms to various forces in El Salvador by any country has already been stated. We oppose it and we hope
that the problems of El Salvador can be solved peacefully by the people of El Salvador without outside interference.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: FINANCE-EFFECT OF BUDGET ON EMPLOYEES MEETING INCREASED ACCOMMODATION COSTS FOLLOWING TRANSFERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PROVISION AFFECTING MORTGAGES BE POSTPONED
FINANCE-EFFECT OF BUDGET ON EMPLOYEES MEETING INCREASED ACCOMMODATION COSTS FOLLOWING TRANSFERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PROVISION AFFECTING MORTGAGES BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. 1 welcome this opportunity to deal at some greater length with questions which I raised in the House on January 29 and the replies that I received thereto. Those questions dealt with the intended amendments to section 80.4(1) of the Income Tax Act, referable to-as they now provide-the exemption from the inclusion in income of the alleged benefits to employees of employer-provided mortgages at either no interest or at interest rates which are less than the going rate. I raise these issues because of responses provided to me by the minister. At page 14462 and 14463 of Hansard the minister's responses are to the effect that he takes my questions as representations and notes that they will be considered in due course. That answer underlines, regrettably, the way in which the entire budget was prepared. It was prepared as though a white paper on major tax reform had preceded it, without regard to the fact that there are elements in society very substantially affected by the intended budget proposals. One of those provisions is the one to which 1 made reference, and if I could just read some of the communications I have received from my constituents with respect to this matter hon. members would get a better grasp of the consequences of the intended amendment to that section of the Income Tax Act. I do not propose to refer to the names of the people who have actually corresponded with me because some of the letters have been marked "personal and confidential", and some of them have disclosed personal financial information which the writers might prefer I not read into the record because that would identify them as the people who have this particular problem. However, one letter dated December 8, 1981 contains the following comment:
As a direct result of the new provisions in the November 12th, 1981 budget, the tax payable on my interest-free loan will add $320 to my monthly payments. This increase would leave me no alternative but to sell my house, at a direct cost to myself of the 6 per cent sales commission, and moving expenses.
This is just one of the cases, but, as a matter of fact, all the cases to which I refer are cases in which individual taxpayers have been transferred by their employers to new locations under circumstances wherein the cost of acquiring new residences exceeded the cost at former locations.
The gentleman went on to say:
At the time of my transfer, my decision to relocate was based on the provisions of The Income Tax Act in effect at that time.
1 believe that in the interests of fairness it would be only just and reasonable to withdraw the imposition of this tax on loans already in place at the time of the budget, allowing the new measure to affect only those loans negotiated after that date.
February 1, 1982

Another gentleman stated in a letter also dated December 8, 1981:
The most disturbing factor is the retroactivity of this legislation which disturbs the agreement reached with my employer at the time of my transfer.
This gentleman also stated:
One of the conditions set by the Foreign Investment Review Agency-
This was at the time his employer acquired the stock of another corporation of which this gentleman is a former employee.
-required the company to ensure that no employees were to be dismissed as a result of the acquisition and in order to comply with this condition it was necessary to move a number of individuals into various locations in Canada. In most cases the transfers were to areas where substantial differentials existed on housing costs.
He gave the example of Montreal as against Toronto.
One of the principal themes of the federal budget introduced on November 12, 1981, was the question of equity and the need to maintain a fundamental sense of fairness in our country. I believe that in the interests of fairness it would be only just and reasonable to withdraw the imposition of this tax on loans already in place-
It is interesting that one of my constituents gave the specific example of having moved from the city of Beaconsfield, Quebec where his monthly payment on his residence at that time totalled $ 166 per month. He moved to a home of comparable value in terms of what it would provide him compared with what he was provided in Beaconsfield and found that his total costs, even with his interest-free and interest-reduced loans, amounted to $1,199 per month. In the event that these proposals of the budget are to be implemented he will be confronted with an additional cost because the total amount of his loans is now $78,000, and he must pay tax on $10,729 of that. He has not given me his tax rate, but assuming it is 30 per cent, that will total $3,000 more he will have to pay, in addition to his current monthly payment.
All of these moves have been undertaken as a consequence of the requirement of the employer and not the employee, Mr. Speaker. Whatever benefit accrues, will accrue to the employer who now has an employee who has moved to a new location, a move sought by the employer and not the employee.
One of the letters that 1 received made reference to a specific paragraph on page 21 of the budget papers which reads as follows:
Housing loans mainly provide benefits to mobile, high-income employees and officers of corporations and amount to an indirect subsidy for industries who regularly relocate their employees.
This gentleman is an employee of a firm that has only changed its location once. He has never changed his location and has always been an employee of that same corporation. He denies that he is at an upper income level.
Some time ago this House passed a resolution dealing with the Constitution and under Paragraph 6.(2) granted to every Canadian the right to move to and take up residence in any province in pursuit of a livelihood in any province. That right becomes very shallow when the financial obligation imposed upon these people when they move under the provision of the budget will specifically preclude them from undertaking the steps allegedly granted under this resolution which will become part of the Constitution of Canada.
Adjournment Debate
I submit that in the event that equity and fairness is to prevail, arrangements arrived at between employees and employers with respect to this issue be left until they run their due course. In that way the people of Canada will enjoy fairness and equity.
Mir. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, this motion concerns budget changes to the provision which permitted employers to provide up to $50,000 of interest-free loans to employees who relocated without the resulting benefit being subject to income tax. The budget proposes to eliminate this measure effective for the 1982 taxation year. A transition rule will allow benefits on up to $40,000 of existing loans to be exempt in 1982, and this limit is reduced to $20,000 for 1983. Certainly relocation and labour mobility are desirable. However, this measure was not a particularly effective or fair one. There are a number of reasons why it was terminated.
Housing loans are but one method of remunerating employees for differences in costs of living resulting from a relocation. Others include promotions or increased pay, which generally occur on relocation, cash payments to offset differences in the mortgage interest rate on the new versus the old home, rental cost subsidies and general cost of living wage differences between regions.
Conference board data show that over half of firms do not offer tax subsidized housing loans. Most that do, do not make them available to all employees. Moreover, a significant number of firms offer other types of remuneration for relocation that have always been taxable. These facts raise serious questions of equity in existing housing loans.
As well, housing loans did not assist persons already living in a region with their higher living costs. They had to meet these costs out of taxable wages and salaries. Housing loans could actually reduce labour market mobility as they intended to lock employees into a job with the firm that provided them the loan. Higher income employees were more likely to get a loan, were more likely to get a loan for a higher amount, and derived more tax savings per dollar of loan than did a taxpayer in a lower tax bracket. Lastly, in some regions the measure may have added significantly to upward pressure on home prices. I do not believe that a measure with these sorts of defects can be justified.
The budget does not prohibit the use of housing loans for this purpose and I expect the past practice to continue. Interest-free housing loans continue to be attractive. Employees will not have to pay interest but only tax on the benefit-on the interest-free amount. What ordinary Canadian in a 30 per cent tax bracket can obtain a $50,000 mortgage loan at an annual cost of $2,400, compared to the current market cost of roughly $8,500 to any other Canadian?
